optionC: Propagation across the geomagnetic equator
optionD: Signals reflected back toward the transmitting station
explanation: Chordal hop is when a signal is refracted from one region of the ionosphere to another, again and again, without coming down to the ground in between. It is not about leaving the great-circle bearing or crossing the geomagnetic equator.

question: Which of the following is indicated by a sudden rise in radio background noise across a large portion of the HF spectrum?
optionB: A coronal mass ejection impact or a solar flare has occurred
optionC: Transequatorial propagation on 6 meters is likely
optionD: Long-path propagation on the higher HF bands is likely
explanation: A sudden jump in background noise across much of HF suggests that a solar flare or the arrival of a coronal mass ejection has disturbed the ionosphere and geomagnetic field. A temperature inversion affects VHF and up, not wideband HF noise.

question: Which of these emission modes is best for auroral propagation?
optionC: FM
explanation: Signals reflected from the moving aurora are smeared by Doppler spread and sound raspy and distorted, so voice and RTTY become hard to copy. CW keeps working because the operator only needs to hear the tone come and go, and it fits a narrow bandwidth.

question: What type of polarization is supported by ground-wave propagation?
optionC: Circular
explanation: Ground waves need vertical polarization, because horizontally polarized waves near the ground are largely shorted out by the Earth. That is why AM broadcast and other ground-wave services use vertical antennas.

question: What are circularly polarized electromagnetic waves?
optionA: Waves with an electric field bent into a circular shape
optionB: Waves with rotating electric and magnetic fields
optionC: Waves that circle Earth
optionD: Waves produced by a loop antenna
explanation: In a circularly polarized wave the electric and magnetic fields rotate around the direction of travel, making one full turn each cycle. The field is not bent into a circle, and the name has nothing to do with waves circling Earth.

question: Which of the following limits the highest frequency signal that can be accurately displayed on a digital oscilloscope?
optionA: Sampling rate of the analog-to-digital converter
optionC: Q of the circuit
explanation: A digital scope can only represent signals below half its sampling rate, the Nyquist limit, so the sampling rate of its analog-to-digital converter sets the highest frequency it can show accurately. The circuit's Q has nothing to do with it.

question: Which of the following factors most affects the accuracy of a frequency counter?
optionC: Decade divider accuracy
explanation: Every frequency counter reading is measured against its internal time base, so any error in that reference shows up directly in the reading. That is why good counters use a temperature-controlled or GPS-disciplined reference oscillator.

question: What is an effect of excessive phase noise in an SDR receiver's master clock oscillator?
optionA: It limits the receiver's ability to receive strong signals
optionB: It can affect the receiver's frequency calibration
optionC: It decreases the receiver's third-order intercept point
optionD: It can combine with strong signals on nearby frequencies to generate interference
explanation: Phase noise on the master clock spreads noise sidebands around every signal the receiver mixes. A strong signal nearby can then mix with those sidebands and drop noise onto the frequency you are listening to, which is reciprocal mixing.

question: What is meant by the blocking dynamic range of a receiver?
optionA: The difference in dB between the noise floor and the level of an incoming signal that will cause 1 dB of gain compression
optionB: The minimum difference in dB between the levels of two FM signals that will cause one signal to block the other
optionC: The difference in dB between the noise floor and the third-order intercept point
optionD: The minimum difference in dB between two signals which produce third-order intermodulation products greater than the noise floor
explanation: Blocking dynamic range is the span in dB from the receiver's noise floor up to the level of an off-frequency signal that causes 1 dB of gain compression. It shows how strong a nearby signal can be before the wanted signal is weakened.

question: What problem can occur when using an automatic notch filter (ANF) to remove interfering carriers while receiving CW signals?
optionA: Removal of the CW signal as well as the interfering carrier
optionB: Any nearby signal passing through the DSP system will overwhelm the desired signal
optionC: Excessive ringing
explanation: An automatic notch filter looks for steady tones and removes them. A CW signal is also a steady tone, so the filter may notch out the station you want along with the interfering carrier. That is why ANF is usually turned off for CW.

question: Which of the following parameters does a spectrum analyzer display on the vertical and horizontal axes?
optionC: SWR and frequency
explanation: A spectrum analyzer shows signal amplitude on the vertical axis against frequency on the horizontal axis. That frequency-domain view is what separates it from an oscilloscope, which plots amplitude against time.

question: What is the significance of voltmeter sensitivity expressed in ohms per volt?
optionA: The full scale reading of the voltmeter multiplied by its ohms per volt rating is the input impedance of the voltmeter
optionB: The reading in volts multiplied by the ohms per volt rating will determine the power drawn by the device under test
optionC: The reading in ohms divided by the ohms per volt rating will determine the voltage applied to the circuit
optionD: The full scale reading in amps divided by ohms per volt rating will determine the size of shunt needed
explanation: For an analog meter, input resistance = full-scale voltage x ohms per volt. A 20,000 ohms per volt meter on its 10 V range presents 10 x 20,000 = 200,000 ohms, so a higher rating loads the circuit less.

question: Which of the following receiver circuits can be effective in eliminating interference from strong out-of-band signals?
optionC: A notch filter
explanation: A preselector or front-end filter stops strong signals outside the band before they reach the first amplifier or mixer, where they would cause overload. A narrow IF filter only acts after those stages, too late to help.

question: Which of the following describes problems caused by poor dynamic range in a receiver?
optionA: Spurious signals caused by cross modulation and desensitization from strong adjacent signals
optionB: Oscillator instability requiring frequent retuning and loss of ability to recover the opposite sideband
optionC: Poor weak signal reception caused by insufficient local oscillator injection
optionD: Oscillator instability and severe audio distortion of all but the strongest received signals
explanation: With poor dynamic range, strong signals near your frequency overload the front end, causing cross modulation, where their modulation appears on other signals, and desensitization, where weak signals fade. Oscillator stability has nothing to do with it.

question: Which of the following types of noise can often be reduced by a digital noise reduction?
optionC: Power line noise
explanation: DSP noise reduction can often lower broadband white noise, ignition noise and power line noise, since it separates signal from noise statistically. How well it works varies, but it can help with each.

question: Which of the following test instruments is used to display spurious signals and/or intermodulation distortion products generated by an SSB transmitter?
optionC: Logic analyzer
explanation: A spectrum analyzer displays every signal across a range of frequencies, so spurs and intermodulation products next to the SSB signal show up as separate peaks. A logic analyzer reads digital states and cannot show RF products.

question: Which S parameter is equivalent to forward gain?
explanation: In S parameter notation the first subscript is the output port and the second the input port, so S21 compares the signal leaving port 2 with the signal entering port 1. That ratio is the forward gain or transmission.

question: What is the term for the suppression in an FM receiver of one signal by another stronger signal on the same frequency?
optionC: Capture effect
explanation: In FM, the stronger of two signals on the same frequency takes over the demodulator output and the weaker one nearly vanishes. This is the capture effect, which is why FM gives either one station clearly or the other.

question: What creates intermodulation interference between two repeaters in close proximity?
optionA: The output signals cause feedback in the final amplifier of one or both transmitters
optionB: The output signals mix in the final amplifier of one or both transmitters
optionC: The input frequencies are harmonically related
optionD: The output frequencies are harmonically related
explanation: When two repeater transmitters are close together, each one's signal gets into the other's final amplifier, which is nonlinear, and the two mix. The mixing produces new frequencies that can land on a repeater input or another channel.

question: Which of the following types of noise are removed by a noise blanker?
optionC: Hum and buzz
explanation: A noise blanker detects short, strong pulses and mutes the receiver for their brief duration, so it removes impulse noise such as ignition clicks. Continuous noise, hum and buzz carry on between pulses and are not blanked.

question: How is compensation of an oscilloscope probe performed?
optionA: A square wave is displayed, and the probe is adjusted until the horizontal portions of the displayed wave are as nearly flat as possible
optionB: A high frequency sine wave is displayed, and the probe is adjusted for maximum amplitude
optionC: A frequency standard is displayed, and the probe is adjusted until the deflection time is accurate
optionD: A DC voltage standard is displayed, and the probe is adjusted until the displayed voltage is accurate
explanation: To compensate a scope probe you feed it a square wave, usually from the scope's calibrator output, and adjust its small trimmer capacitor until the flat tops and bottoms are neither rounded nor peaked. A flat square wave means the probe passes all frequencies evenly.

question: Which S parameter represents input port return loss or reflection coefficient (equivalent to VSWR)?
explanation: S11 is the signal reflected back out of port 1 compared with the signal sent into port 1. That is the input reflection coefficient, which gives return loss and VSWR. S22 is the same thing measured at the output port.

question: What is the noise figure of a receiver?
optionA: The ratio of atmospheric noise to phase noise
optionB: The ratio of the noise bandwidth in hertz to the theoretical bandwidth of a resistive network
optionC: The ratio in dB of the noise generated in the receiver to atmospheric noise
optionD: The ratio in dB of the noise generated by the receiver to the theoretical minimum noise
explanation: Noise figure is how much noise a receiver adds compared with a perfect, noiseless receiver, expressed in dB. A 3 dB noise figure means the receiver doubles the noise beyond the theoretical minimum. Atmospheric noise is not part of the definition.

question: Which of the following is used to reduce or eliminate intermodulation interference in a repeater caused by a nearby transmitter?
optionA: A band-pass filter in the feed line between the transmitter and receiver
optionB: A properly terminated circulator at the output of the repeater's transmitter
optionC: Utilizing a Class C final amplifier
optionD: Utilizing a Class D final amplifier
explanation: A circulator at the transmitter output passes the outgoing signal to the antenna but sends energy coming back from the antenna into a terminating load. That keeps a nearby transmitter's signal from reaching the final amplifier and mixing there.

question: How can conducted noise from an automobile battery charging system be suppressed?
optionA: By installing filter capacitors in series with the alternator leads
optionB: By installing a noise suppression resistor and a blocking capacitor at the battery
optionC: By installing a high-pass filter in series with the radio's power lead and a low-pass filter in parallel with the antenna feed line
optionD: By installing ferrite chokes on the charging system leads
explanation: Ferrite chokes on the charging system leads block the RF noise the alternator and regulator put out while letting DC charging current pass. Capacitors go across leads to bypass noise, never in series, which would block the charging current.

question: What is the purpose of using a prescaler with a frequency counter?
optionA: Amplify low-level signals for more accurate counting
optionB: Multiply a higher frequency signal so a low-frequency counter can display the operating frequency
optionC: Prevent oscillation in a low-frequency counter circuit
optionD: Reduce the signal frequency to within the counter's operating range
explanation: A prescaler divides the input frequency by a known factor so a high-frequency signal falls within the counter's range, and the reading is then scaled back up. It lowers the frequency, it does not multiply it.

question: What three test loads are used to calibrate an RF vector network analyzer?
optionB: Short circuit, open circuit, and 50 ohms
optionC: Short circuit, open circuit, and resonant circuit
optionD: 50 ohms through 1/8 wavelength, 1/4 wavelength, and 1/2 wavelength of coaxial cable
explanation: A vector network analyzer is calibrated with a short circuit, an open circuit and a precise 50 ohm load, the classic short, open and load standards. Each has a known reflection, so the instrument can remove its own errors.

question: What does a receiver noise floor of -174 dBm represent?
optionA: The receiver noise is 6 dB above the theoretical minimum
optionB: The theoretical noise in a 1 Hz bandwidth at the input of a perfect receiver at room temperature
optionC: The noise figure of a 1 Hz bandwidth receiver
optionD: The receiver noise is 3 dB above theoretical minimum
explanation: Thermal noise power = k x T x B. At 290 K in a 1 Hz bandwidth, 1.38 x 10^-23 x 290 x 1 is about 4.0 x 10^-21 W, which is -174 dBm. A perfect receiver at room temperature cannot have a lower noise floor than that.

question: What is the term for the reduction in receiver sensitivity caused by a strong signal near the received frequency?
optionC: Desensitization
explanation: Desensitization is the loss of receiver sensitivity when a strong signal near your frequency overloads the front end. Weak signals you could copy before become hard to hear even though nothing transmits on your exact frequency.

question: What is used to suppress radio frequency interference from a line-driven AC motor?
optionA: A high-pass filter in series with the motor's power leads
optionB: A brute-force AC-line filter in series with the motor's power leads
optionC: A bypass capacitor in series with the motor's field winding
optionD: A bypass choke in parallel with the motor's field winding
explanation: A brute-force AC-line filter in series with the motor's power leads blocks the RF noise from the brushes before it travels out on the house wiring. A high-pass filter would pass the RF and is the wrong type.

question: What is the effect of aliasing on a digital oscilloscope when displaying a waveform?
optionA: A false, jittery low-frequency version of the waveform is displayed
optionB: The waveform DC offset will be inaccurate
optionC: Calibration of the vertical scale is no longer valid
optionD: Excessive blanking occurs, which prevents display of the waveform
explanation: When a signal is sampled too slowly, the samples trace out a false lower-frequency waveform that may look unstable or jittery on screen. That is aliasing. The vertical calibration and DC offset are not what it affects.

question: How much power is being absorbed by the load when a directional power meter connected between a transmitter and a terminating load reads 100 watts forward power and 25 watts reflected power?
optionC: 112.5 watts
explanation: Power into the load = forward power - reflected power = 100 W - 25 W = 75 W. Adding the two to get 125 W is the common mistake; the reflected power is returning toward the transmitter, not reaching the load.

question: How much does increasing a receiver's bandwidth from 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz increase the receiver's noise floor?
optionC: 10 dB
explanation: Noise power rises in proportion to bandwidth, so the increase = 10 log(1,000 / 50) = 10 log(20), about 13 dB. Going from 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz lets in 20 times as much noise.

question: Which of the following reduces the likelihood of receiver desensitization?
optionA: Insert attenuation before the first RF stage
optionC: Increase the receiver's front-end gain
optionD: Switch from fast AGC to slow AGC
explanation: Adding attenuation before the first RF stage lowers the strong signal to a level the front end can handle, so it stops overloading. Increasing front-end gain would make desensitization worse.

question: What type of electrical interference can be caused by computer network equipment?
optionA: A loud AC hum in the audio output of your station's receiver
optionB: A clicking noise at intervals of a few seconds
optionC: The appearance of unstable modulated or unmodulated signals at specific frequencies
optionD: A whining-type noise that continually pulses off and on
explanation: Computer network equipment uses clock and data signals that can radiate, appearing in a receiver as steady carriers, modulated or not, at fixed frequencies, often drifting a little. A whining or clicking noise points to other sources.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of using an antenna analyzer compared to an SWR bridge?
optionA: Antenna analyzers automatically tune your antenna for resonance
optionB: Antenna analyzers compute SWR and impedance automatically
optionC: Antenna analyzers display a time-varying representation of the modulation envelope
explanation: An antenna analyzer works out SWR and impedance for you, often across a sweep of frequencies. It does not tune the antenna for you and does not show a modulation envelope.

question: What do the subscripts of S parameters represent?
optionA: The port or ports at which measurements are made
optionC: Relative quality of the data
explanation: The two digits after the S name the ports involved: the first is the port where the signal is measured and the second the port where it is applied. They say nothing about timing or data quality.

question: What does the MDS of a receiver represent?
optionC: The modulation distortion specification
explanation: MDS stands for minimum discernible signal, the weakest signal the receiver can detect, usually defined as the level that equals its noise floor in a given bandwidth. It is a common sensitivity rating in receiver reviews.

question: What causes intermodulation in an electronic circuit?
optionC: Nonlinear circuits or devices
explanation: Intermodulation happens when signals pass through a nonlinear circuit or device, which creates sum and difference products such as 2f1 - f2. A perfectly linear circuit would pass the signals without mixing them.

question: Which of the following can cause shielded cables to radiate or receive interference?
optionA: Low inductance ground connections at both ends of the shield
optionB: Common-mode currents on the shield and conductors
optionC: Use of braided shielding material
optionD: Tying all ground connections to a common point resulting in differential-mode currents in the shield
explanation: When common-mode current flows on a cable's shield and conductors together, the whole cable acts like an antenna and can radiate or pick up interference. Low-inductance shield grounds at both ends and braided shields are normal good practice.

question: Which of the following is used to measure SWR?
optionC: Antenna analyzer
explanation: A directional wattmeter, a vector network analyzer and an antenna analyzer can each measure SWR. The wattmeter derives it from forward and reflected power, and the analyzers measure the reflection directly.

question: Which of the following can be used to determine the Q of a series-tuned circuit?
optionA: The ratio of inductive reactance to capacitive reactance
optionC: The bandwidth of the circuit's frequency response
optionD: The resonant frequency of the circuit
explanation: Q of a tuned circuit = resonant frequency / bandwidth between its half-power points. A circuit resonant at 7 MHz with a 70 kHz bandwidth has Q = 7,000 / 70 = 100, so measuring the bandwidth of the response gives Q.

question: An SDR receiver is overloaded when input signals exceed what level?
optionA: One-half of the maximum sample rate
optionB: One-half of the maximum sampling buffer size
optionC: The maximum count value of the analog-to-digital converter
optionD: The reference voltage of the analog-to-digital converter
explanation: An SDR's analog-to-digital converter can only represent voltages up to its reference voltage. Signals that go beyond it clip, which causes distortion and spurious signals across the band. The sample rate has nothing to do with overload.

question: What is the purpose of the preselector in a communications receiver?
optionA: To store frequencies that are often used
optionB: To provide broadband attenuation before the first RF stage to prevent intermodulation
optionC: To increase the rejection of signals outside the band being received
optionD: To allow selection of the optimum RF amplifier device
explanation: A preselector is a tuned filter ahead of the receiver that passes the band you are using and rejects signals outside it. It improves image rejection and keeps strong out-of-band signals from overloading the front end.

question: What current flows equally on all conductors of an unshielded multiconductor cable?
optionC: Reactive current only
explanation: Common-mode current flows in the same direction and amount on every conductor of a cable, so the cable behaves like a single wire. Differential-mode current is the normal signal, flowing out on one conductor and back on another.

question: Which of the following is good practice when using an oscilloscope probe?
optionA: Minimize the length of the probe's ground connection
optionB: Never use a high-impedance probe to measure a low-impedance circuit
optionC: Never use a DC-coupled probe to measure an AC circuit
explanation: Keep the probe ground lead as short as you can, because a long ground lead adds inductance that causes ringing and overshoot on fast signals. The other statements are not real rules; high-impedance and DC-coupled probes are used all the time.

question: Which of the following can be measured by a two-port vector network analyzer?
optionC: Pulse rise time
explanation: A two-port vector network analyzer sweeps a signal through a device and measures what comes out and what reflects, so it can show a filter's frequency response, including loss and phase. Phase noise and pulse rise time need other instruments.

question: Which of the following choices is a good reason for selecting a high IF for a superheterodyne HF or VHF communications receiver?
optionC: Easier for front-end circuitry to eliminate image responses
explanation: A high IF puts the image frequency far from the wanted signal, since the image sits two times the IF away. A front-end filter can then remove the image easily. A high IF does not by itself improve noise figure or reduce drift.

question: What does a third-order intercept level of 40 dBm mean with respect to receiver performance?
optionA: Signals less than 40 dBm will not generate audible third-order intermodulation products
optionB: The receiver can tolerate signals up to 40 dB above the noise floor without producing third-order intermodulation products
optionC: A pair of 40 dBm input signals will theoretically generate a third-order intermodulation product that has the same output amplitude as either of the input signals
optionD: A pair of 1 mW input signals will produce a third-order intermodulation product that is 40 dB stronger than the input signal
explanation: The third-order intercept point is where the extended lines for the wanted output and the third-order products would meet. At 40 dBm, two 40 dBm input signals would in theory produce third-order products as strong as each of the signals.

question: What undesirable effect can occur when using a noise blanker?
optionA: Received audio in the speech range might have an echo effect
optionB: The audio frequency bandwidth of the received signal might be compressed
optionC: Strong signals may be distorted and appear to cause spurious emissions
optionD: FM signals can no longer be demodulated
explanation: A noise blanker reacts to strong pulses, and a very strong nearby signal can trigger it, chopping the signal and creating distortion products that seem to spread across the band. Turning the blanker off clears this up.

question: Which trigger mode is most effective when using an oscilloscope to measure a linear power supply's output ripple?
optionC: Level
explanation: Ripple on a linear supply comes from the AC mains frequency, so line triggering, which locks the sweep to the AC line, gives a steady trace of it. Edge or level triggering may not lock well on a small, noisy ripple riding on DC.

question: Which of the following methods measures intermodulation distortion in an SSB transmitter?
optionA: Modulate the transmitter using two RF signals having non-harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a spectrum analyzer
optionB: Modulate the transmitter using two AF signals having non-harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a spectrum analyzer
optionC: Modulate the transmitter using two AF signals having harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a peak reading wattmeter
optionD: Modulate the transmitter using two RF signals having harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a logic analyzer
explanation: The standard two-tone test drives the SSB transmitter with two audio tones that are not harmonically related, then looks at the RF output on a spectrum analyzer. Any intermodulation shows up as extra signals spaced beside the two tones.

question: What is an advantage of having a variety of receiver bandwidths from which to select?
optionA: The noise figure of the RF amplifier can be adjusted to match the modulation type, thus increasing receiver sensitivity
optionB: Receiver power consumption can be reduced when wider bandwidth is not required
optionC: Receive bandwidth can be set to match the modulation bandwidth, maximizing signal-to-noise ratio and minimizing interference
optionD: Multiple frequencies can be received simultaneously if desired
explanation: Matching the receive bandwidth to the signal, narrow for CW and wider for SSB, lets in all of the wanted signal while keeping out extra noise and nearby stations. That gives the best signal-to-noise ratio and the least interference.

question: Why are odd-order intermodulation products, created within a receiver, of particular interest compared to other products?
optionA: Odd-order products of two signals in the band being received are also likely to be within the band
optionB: Odd-order products are more likely to overload the IF filters
optionC: Odd-order products are an indication of poor image rejection
optionD: Odd-order intermodulation produces three products for every input signal within the band of interest
explanation: Odd-order products such as 2f1 - f2 fall near the original signals. Two signals at 14.010 and 14.020 MHz give products at 14.000 and 14.030 MHz, still in the band, while even-order products land far away.

question: Which of the following can create intermittent loud roaring or buzzing AC line interference?
optionA: Arcing contacts in a thermostatically controlled device
optionB: A defective doorbell or doorbell transformer inside a nearby residence
optionC: A malfunctioning illuminated advertising display
explanation: Arcing thermostat contacts, a faulty doorbell or its transformer, and a failing lighted sign can each produce intermittent loud roaring or buzzing on the AC line. Any arcing in AC wiring can do it.

question: Which of the following can be measured with an antenna analyzer?
optionC: Resonant frequency of a tuned circuit
explanation: An antenna analyzer can measure a feed line's velocity factor and its length, and it can find the resonant frequency of a tuned circuit. All three come from how impedance changes with frequency.

question: Which of the following can be measured with a vector network analyzer?
optionC: Reflection coefficient
explanation: A vector network analyzer measures both magnitude and phase of reflected and transmitted signals, so it can find input impedance, output impedance and the reflection coefficient. All three are standard measurements.

question: Why does input attenuation reduce receiver overload on the lower frequency HF bands with little or no impact on signal-to-noise ratio?
optionA: The attenuator has a low-pass filter to increase the strength of lower frequency signals
optionB: The attenuator has a noise filter to suppress interference
optionC: Signals are attenuated separately from the noise
optionD: Atmospheric noise is generally greater than internally generated noise even after attenuation
explanation: On the low HF bands, atmospheric noise is usually far stronger than the receiver's own noise. An attenuator lowers signal and atmospheric noise together, and that noise still stays above the receiver's noise, so the signal-to-noise ratio barely changes while overload is reduced.

question: What is the link margin in a system with a transmit power level of 10 W (+40 dBm), a system antenna gain of 10 dBi, a cable loss of 3 dB, a path loss of 136 dB, a receiver minimum discernable signal of -103 dBm, and a required signal-to-noise ratio of 6 dB?
optionC: +8dB
explanation: Received level = 40 + 10 - 3 - 136 = -89 dBm. The level needed is the MDS plus the required SNR, -103 + 6 = -97 dBm. Link margin = -89 - (-97) = +8 dB.

question: What could be the cause of local AM broadcast band signals combining to generate spurious signals on the MF or HF bands?
optionA: One or more of the broadcast stations is transmitting an over-modulated signal
optionB: Nearby corroded metal connections are mixing and reradiating the broadcast signals
optionC: You are receiving skywave signals from a distant station
optionD: Your station receiver IF amplifier stage is overloaded
explanation: Corroded metal joints can act like crude diodes, so strong local broadcast signals mix in them and the products are reradiated on other frequencies. This is the rusty bolt effect. Over-modulation would not combine two stations.

question: How does a narrow-band roofing filter affect receiver performance?
optionA: It improves sensitivity by reducing front-end noise
optionB: It improves intelligibility by using low Q circuitry to reduce ringing
optionC: It improves blocking dynamic range by attenuating strong signals near the receive frequency
explanation: A roofing filter is a narrow filter right after the first mixer that keeps strong signals near the receive frequency out of later stages. That raises the receiver's blocking dynamic range. It does not lower front-end noise.

question: What is the received signal level with a transmit power of 10 W (+40 dBm), a transmit antenna gain of 6 dBi, a receive antenna gain of 3 dBi, and a path loss of 100 dB?
optionC: -57 dBm
explanation: Received level = transmit power + transmit antenna gain + receive antenna gain - path loss = 40 + 6 + 3 - 100 = -51 dBm. All the figures are in dB, so they simply add and subtract.

question: What causes interference received as a series of carriers at regular intervals across a wide frequency range?
optionC: Wireless security camera transmitters
explanation: Switch-mode power supplies switch at a fixed rate and produce harmonics at regular spacing, heard as a series of carriers marching across a wide frequency range. Radar and electric fences produce pulses or clicks instead.

question: What is reciprocal mixing?
optionA: Two out-of-band signals mixing to generate an in-band spurious signal
optionB: In-phase signals cancelling in a mixer resulting in loss of receiver sensitivity
optionC: Two digital signals combining from alternate time slots
optionD: Local oscillator phase noise mixing with adjacent strong signals to create interference to desired signals
explanation: In reciprocal mixing, noise from the receiver's local oscillator mixes with a strong signal close to the one you want, putting noise into your passband. The phase noise on the oscillator causes it, not two out-of-band signals combining.

question: What power level does a receiver minimum discernible signal of -100 dBm represent?
optionC: 0.001 microwatts
explanation: P = 1 mW x 10^(-100/10) = 10^-3 x 10^-10 W = 10^-13 W, which is 0.1 picowatt. Each 10 dB below 0 dBm divides the power by ten.

question: Where should a station AC surge protector be installed?
optionC: On the single point ground panel
optionD: On a ground rod outside the station
explanation: The surge protector for station AC belongs on the single point ground panel, so that it and every other protector share one ground reference. Bonding them together keeps transients from creating voltage differences between equipment.

question: What is the purpose of the receiver IF Shift control?
optionA: To permit listening on a different frequency from the transmitting frequency
optionC: To reduce interference from stations transmitting on adjacent frequencies
optionD: To tune in stations slightly off frequency without changing the transmit frequency
explanation: IF Shift slides the IF passband up or down relative to the signal without changing the tuned frequency. You can move the filter edge away from a station just beside yours, reducing interference while staying on frequency.

question: What is the purpose of a single point ground panel?
optionA: Remove AC power in case of a short-circuit
optionB: Prevent common-mode transients in multi-wire systems
optionC: Eliminate air gaps between protected and non-protected circuits
optionD: Ensure all lightning protectors activate at the same time
explanation: A single point ground panel bonds every protector, for feed lines, rotator cables and AC, to one common ground. During a lightning surge they all rise to the same potential and activate together, so no damaging voltage builds up between them.

question: What can cause the voltage across reactances in a series RLC circuit to be higher than the voltage applied to the entire circuit?
optionC: Low quality factor (Q)
explanation: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, so only the small resistance limits current. That large current flowing through each reactance develops a voltage across it that can be many times the applied voltage. A low Q would do the opposite and keep those voltages small.

question: What is the term for the time required for the capacitor in an RC circuit to be charged to 63.2% of the applied voltage or to discharge to 36.8% of its initial voltage?
optionC: One exponential period
explanation: One time constant (R x C seconds) is the time for a capacitor to charge to 63.2% of the applied voltage, or discharge to 36.8% of its starting voltage. After about five time constants it is essentially fully charged or discharged.

question: Which of the following represents pure capacitive reactance of 100 ohms in rectangular notation?
explanation: In rectangular form the real part is resistance and the imaginary part is reactance, with capacitive reactance negative. A pure 100 ohm capacitive reactance has zero resistance, so it is written 0 - j100. Plus j100 would be inductive.

question: What is the result of conductor skin effect?
optionA: Resistance increases as frequency increases because RF current flows closer to the surface
optionB: Resistance decreases as frequency increases because electron mobility increases
optionC: Resistance increases as temperature increases because of the change in thermal coefficient
optionD: Resistance decreases as temperature increases because of the change in thermal coefficient
explanation: As frequency rises, RF current crowds toward the outer surface of a conductor, so less of the cross section carries it and the effective resistance goes up. That is why RF conductors are often wide straps or plated with silver.

question: What is the resonant frequency of an RLC circuit if R is 22 ohms, L is 50 microhenries, and C is 40 picofarads?
optionC: 3.56 MHz
explanation: f = 1 / (2 x pi x sqrt(L x C)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x sqrt(50e-6 x 40e-12)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x 4.472e-8) = 1 / 2.81e-7, about 3.56 MHz. Resistance does not change the resonant frequency, so the 22 ohms is not used.

question: What letter is commonly used to represent susceptance?
optionC: Y
explanation: Susceptance, the imaginary part of admittance, is written with the letter B. G is conductance, Y is admittance as a whole, and X is reactance.

question: How are impedances described in polar coordinates?
optionC: By magnitude and phase angle
explanation: Polar coordinates describe an impedance by its magnitude (total ohms) and its phase angle. Real and imaginary parts, or R and X values, are the rectangular way of writing the same impedance.

question: Why is it important to keep lead lengths short for components used in circuits for VHF and above?
optionA: To increase the thermal time constant
optionC: To maintain component lifetime
explanation: Every bit of lead has inductance, and at VHF and higher the reactance of even a short lead (XL = 2 x pi x f x L) becomes significant. Keeping leads short minimizes that unwanted inductive reactance and the coupling it causes.

question: What is the magnitude of the impedance of a series RLC circuit at resonance?
optionA: High, compared to the circuit resistance
optionC: Approximately equal to inductive reactance
explanation: In a series RLC circuit at resonance, XL and XC are equal and opposite, so they cancel. What remains is the circuit resistance, which is why the impedance is at its minimum and roughly equal to R rather than to either reactance.

question: How is impedance in polar form converted to an equivalent admittance?
optionA: Take the reciprocal of the angle and change the sign of the magnitude
optionB: Take the reciprocal of the magnitude and change the sign of the angle
optionC: Take the square root of the magnitude and add 180 degrees to the angle
optionD: Square the magnitude and subtract 90 degrees from the angle
explanation: Admittance is 1 divided by impedance. In polar form you take the reciprocal of the magnitude and change the sign of the phase angle, so 50 ohms at +30 degrees becomes 0.02 siemens at -30 degrees.

question: Which of the following represents a pure inductive reactance in polar coordinates?
optionC: A positive 90 degree phase angle
explanation: A pure inductive reactance has voltage leading current by a full 90 degrees, so in polar form it sits at a positive 90 degree angle. A negative 90 degree angle would be a pure capacitive reactance, and 45 degrees means equal resistance and reactance.

question: What is the phase relationship between current and voltage for reactive power?
optionC: They are 90 degrees out of phase
optionD: They are 45 degrees out of phase
explanation: Reactive power exists when current and voltage are 90 degrees out of phase, as in a pure inductor or capacitor. Energy flows in and back out each cycle, so the average power is zero. In-phase current and voltage would be real power.

question: What is the magnitude of the impedance of a parallel RLC circuit at resonance?
optionC: Low compared to the circuit resistance
optionD: High compared to the circuit resistance
explanation: At parallel resonance the inductive and capacitive branch currents are equal and opposite, so the LC combination looks like a very high impedance. The source then sees mainly the resistance, so the impedance magnitude is approximately the circuit resistance.

question: What is the time constant of a circuit having two 220-microfarad capacitors and two 1-megohm resistors, all in parallel?
optionC: 440 seconds
explanation: Two 220 uF capacitors in parallel give 440 uF, and two 1 megohm resistors in parallel give 0.5 megohm. Time constant = R x C = 500,000 x 0.000440 = 220 seconds.

question: What type of Y-axis scale is most often used for graphs of circuit frequency response?
optionC: Random
explanation: Frequency response plots usually put gain or attenuation on a logarithmic scale, often in decibels, because responses span many orders of magnitude. A linear axis would squeeze the small values near zero.

question: Why are short connections used at microwave frequencies?
optionB: To reduce phase shift along the connection
optionC: To increase compensating capacitance
explanation: At microwave frequencies a connection only a few millimeters long is a noticeable fraction of a wavelength, so it adds phase shift. Short connections keep that phase shift, and the impedance changes it causes, small.

question: What is the result of increasing the Q of an impedance-matching circuit?
optionC: Losses increase
explanation: Bandwidth equals the center frequency divided by Q, so raising the Q of a matching network narrows the range of frequencies it matches well. A higher Q network is sharper, not broader, and it tends to suppress harmonics rather than add them.

question: What is the effect on the magnitude of pure reactance when it is converted to susceptance?
optionC: It is shifted by 90 degrees
optionD: It is replaced by its reciprocal
explanation: Susceptance is the reciprocal of reactance (B = 1 / X), so converting a pure reactance to susceptance replaces its magnitude with the reciprocal. A 50 ohm reactance becomes 0.02 siemens of susceptance.

question: What kind of diagram is used to show the phase relationship between impedances at a given frequency?
optionC: Phasor diagram
explanation: A phasor diagram draws impedances, voltages or currents as arrows whose length is magnitude and whose angle is phase at one frequency. A Venn diagram shows set overlap and has nothing to do with phase.

question: What parasitic characteristic causes electrolytic capacitors to be unsuitable for use at RF?
optionC: Inductance
explanation: Electrolytic capacitors are built from long rolled foils, giving them substantial series inductance. At RF that inductance dominates, so the part no longer behaves like a capacitor. That is why they are used for power supply and audio bypassing, not RF.

question: What is the magnitude of the circulating current within the components of a parallel LC circuit at resonance?
optionC: It equals 1 divided by the quantity 2 times pi, times the square root of (inductance L multiplied by capacitance C)
optionD: It equals 2 times pi, times the square root of (inductance L multiplied by capacitance C)
explanation: In a parallel LC tank at resonance, energy swings back and forth between the coil and the capacitor, so the current circulating inside the loop is at its maximum, often Q times the line current. The formula involving 2 pi and the square root of LC gives frequency, not current.

question: What is susceptance?
optionA: The magnetic impedance of a circuit
optionB: The ratio of magnetic field to electric field
optionC: The imaginary part of admittance
optionD: A measure of the efficiency of a transformer
explanation: Admittance is written Y = G + jB, where G is conductance and B is susceptance. Susceptance is therefore the imaginary part of admittance, the reactive counterpart of conductance, measured in siemens.

question: What does the impedance 50 - j25 ohms represent?
optionA: 50 ohms resistance in series with 25 ohms inductive reactance
optionB: 50 ohms resistance in series with 25 ohms capacitive reactance
optionC: 25 ohms resistance in series with 50 ohms inductive reactance
optionD: 25 ohms resistance in series with 50 ohms capacitive reactance
explanation: In R + jX notation the real part, 50, is resistance and the imaginary part, -25, is reactance. A negative j term is capacitive, so this is 50 ohms of resistance in series with 25 ohms of capacitive reactance.

question: What parasitic characteristic creates an inductor's self-resonance?
optionC: Coupling
explanation: The turns of a coil sit side by side with small capacitance between them. That inter-turn capacitance resonates with the coil's own inductance at some frequency, its self-resonant frequency, above which the part acts like a capacitor.

question: What is the magnitude of the current at the input of a parallel RLC circuit at resonance?
optionC: R/L
explanation: A parallel resonant circuit presents its highest impedance at resonance, so the current drawn from the source is at a minimum there, even though a large current circulates inside the tank itself.

question: What is the phase angle between the voltage across and the current through a series RLC circuit if XC is 500 ohms, R is 1 kilohm, and XL is 250 ohms?
optionA: 68.2 degrees with the voltage leading the current
optionB: 14.0 degrees with the voltage leading the current
optionC: 14.0 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
optionD: 68.2 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
explanation: Net reactance = XL - XC = 250 - 500 = -250 ohms, which is capacitive. Angle = arctan(250 / 1000) = 14.0 degrees. Because the circuit is capacitive, the current leads, so the voltage lags the current by 14.0 degrees.

question: Where is the impedance of a pure resistance plotted on rectangular coordinates?
optionB: On a line through the origin, slanted at 45 degrees
optionC: On a horizontal line, offset vertically above the horizontal axis
explanation: On rectangular impedance coordinates, resistance is on the horizontal axis and reactance on the vertical axis. A pure resistance has no reactance, so it falls right on the horizontal axis.

question: What combines to create the self-resonance of a component?
optionB: The component's nominal and parasitic reactance
optionC: The component's inductance and capacitance
optionD: The component's electrical length and impedance
explanation: Every real component has its intended (nominal) reactance plus unwanted parasitic reactance, such as lead inductance in a capacitor or winding capacitance in a coil. The two resonate together to set the component's self-resonant frequency.

question: What is the phase relationship between the current through and the voltage across a series resonant circuit at resonance?
optionA: The voltage leads the current by 90 degrees
optionB: The current leads the voltage by 90 degrees
optionC: The voltage and current are in phase
optionD: The voltage and current are 180 degrees out of phase
explanation: At resonance the reactances cancel and the series circuit acts like a pure resistance, so voltage and current are in phase. A 90 degree shift would mean a purely reactive load, which is not the case at resonance.

question: What is the phase angle between the voltage across and the current through a series RLC circuit if XC is 300 ohms, R is 100 ohms, and XL is 100 ohms?
optionA: 63 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
optionB: 63 degrees with the voltage leading the current
optionC: 27 degrees with the voltage leading the current
optionD: 27 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
explanation: Net reactance = XL - XC = 100 - 300 = -200 ohms (capacitive). Angle = arctan(200 / 100) = 63.4 degrees, about 63 degrees. A capacitive circuit has the voltage lagging the current.

question: What coordinate system is often used to display the phase angle of a circuit containing resistance, inductive, and/or capacitive reactance?
optionC: Elliptical coordinates
explanation: Polar coordinates show a magnitude and an angle, which makes them a natural way to display the phase angle of a circuit with resistance and reactance. The Maidenhead grid is a locator system for geographic position.

question: What is the primary cause of loss in film capacitors at RF?
optionC: Self-discharge
explanation: Film capacitors use low-loss dielectrics, so at RF most of their loss comes from skin effect raising the resistance of the thin metal plates and leads. Dielectric loss is the tempting choice, but film dielectrics are quite efficient.

question: How is the Q of an RLC parallel resonant circuit calculated?
optionA: Reactance of either the inductance or capacitance divided by the resistance
optionB: Reactance of either the inductance or capacitance multiplied by the resistance
optionC: Resistance divided by the reactance of either the inductance or capacitance
optionD: Reactance of the inductance multiplied by the reactance of the capacitance
explanation: For a parallel resonant circuit, Q = R / X, where X is the reactance of either the inductor or the capacitor (they are equal at resonance). This is the inverse of the series case, where Q = X / R, which is the tempting wrong choice.

question: What is the relationship between the AC current through a capacitor and the voltage across a capacitor?
optionA: Voltage and current are in phase
optionB: Voltage and current are 180 degrees out of phase
optionC: Voltage leads current by 90 degrees
explanation: In a capacitor, current flows to change the charge before the voltage can build, so the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees. The memory aid ELI the ICE man puts I before E for a capacitor (C).

question: When using rectangular coordinates to graph the impedance of a circuit, what do the axes represent?
optionA: The X axis represents the resistive component, and the Y axis represents the reactive component
optionB: The X axis represents the reactive component, and the Y axis represents the resistive component
optionC: The X axis represents the phase angle, and the Y axis represents the magnitude
optionD: The X axis represents the magnitude, and the Y axis represents the phase angle
explanation: When impedance is graphed in rectangular form, the horizontal X axis carries resistance and the vertical Y axis carries reactance, positive for inductive and negative for capacitive. The axes are not magnitude and phase, which belong to polar form.

question: What happens to reactive power in ideal inductors and capacitors?
optionA: It is dissipated as heat in the circuit
optionB: Energy is stored in magnetic or electric fields, but power is not dissipated
optionC: It is canceled by Coulomb forces in the capacitor and inductor
optionD: It is dissipated in the formation of inductive and capacitive fields
explanation: An ideal inductor stores energy in its magnetic field and an ideal capacitor stores it in its electric field, then each returns that energy to the circuit. No energy is dissipated as heat, so reactive power is not consumed.

question: What is the resonant frequency of an RLC circuit if R is 33 ohms, L is 50 microhenries, and C is 10 picofarads?
optionC: 7.12 kHz
explanation: f = 1 / (2 x pi x sqrt(L x C)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x sqrt(50e-6 x 10e-12)) = 1 / (2 x 3.1416 x 2.236e-8) = 1 / 1.405e-7, about 7.12 MHz. The 33 ohm resistance does not affect the resonant frequency.

question: What is the relationship between the AC current through an inductor and the voltage across an inductor?
optionC: Voltage and current are 180 degrees out of phase
optionD: Voltage and current are in phase
explanation: An inductor opposes changes in current, so the voltage across it appears first and the current follows, with voltage leading current by 90 degrees. In ELI the ICE man, E comes before I for an inductor (L).

question: As a conductor's diameter increases, what is the effect on its electrical length?
optionA: Thickness has no effect on electrical length
optionC: It decreases
explanation: A thicker conductor has more capacitance along its length, which slows the wave slightly. So its electrical length, measured in wavelengths, increases and a thick antenna element resonates a little lower than a thin one of the same physical length.

question: What is the half-power bandwidth of a resonant circuit that has a resonant frequency of 7.1 MHz and a Q of 150?
optionC: 47.3 kHz
explanation: Half-power bandwidth = f / Q = 7,100,000 Hz / 150 = 47,333 Hz, about 47.3 kHz. Dividing in the wrong direction or mixing up units gives the much smaller hertz values listed.

question: What is the phase angle between the voltage across and the current through a series RLC circuit if XC is 25 ohms, R is 100 ohms, and XL is 75 ohms?
optionA: 27 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
optionB: 27 degrees with the voltage leading the current
optionC: 63 degrees with the voltage lagging the current
optionD: 63 degrees with the voltage leading the current
explanation: Net reactance = XL - XC = 75 - 25 = +50 ohms, which is inductive. Angle = arctan(50 / 100) = 26.6 degrees, about 27 degrees. In an inductive circuit the voltage leads the current.

question: How much real power is consumed in a circuit consisting of a 100-ohm resistor in series with a 100-ohm inductive reactance drawing 1 ampere?
optionC: 141.4 watts
explanation: Only the resistor dissipates real power. P = I squared x R = 1 x 1 x 100 = 100 watts. The 100 ohm inductive reactance stores and returns energy and adds no real power, so 141.4 watts (the apparent power) is wrong.

question: What is the half-power bandwidth of a resonant circuit that has a resonant frequency of 3.7 MHz and a Q of 118?
optionC: 31.4 kHz
explanation: Half-power bandwidth = f / Q = 3,700,000 Hz / 118 = 31,356 Hz, about 31.4 kHz. Half of that, 15.7 kHz, is the distance from center to one half-power point, not the full bandwidth.

question: What is admittance?
optionB: The term for the gain of a field effect transistor
optionC: The inverse of reactance
optionD: The term for the on-impedance of a field effect transistor
explanation: Admittance (Y) is the inverse of impedance, Y = 1 / Z, measured in siemens. It describes how easily AC flows. The inverse of reactance alone is susceptance, which is only the imaginary part of admittance.

question: What is reactive power?
optionB: Power consumed by an inductor's wire resistance
optionC: The power consumed in inductors and capacitors
explanation: Reactive power is the energy that moves back and forth between a source and inductors or capacitors without being used up, sometimes called wattless or nonproductive power. It is measured in volt-amperes reactive (VAR), not watts.

question: What is an effect of increasing Q in a series resonant circuit?
optionA: Fewer components are needed for the same performance
optionC: Internal voltages increase
explanation: In a series resonant circuit the voltage across each reactance is about Q times the applied voltage, so raising Q raises those internal voltages. Components must be rated to handle them, which is a practical concern in high-Q tuners and filters.

question: In what application is gallium arsenide used as a semiconductor material?
optionC: In microwave circuits
explanation: Gallium arsenide has higher electron mobility than silicon, so devices made from it switch faster and add less noise at very high frequencies. That makes GaAs a common choice for microwave amplifiers and receivers.

question: What is the most useful characteristic of a Zener diode?
optionA: A constant current drop under conditions of varying voltage
optionB: A constant voltage drop under conditions of varying current
optionC: A negative resistance region
optionD: An internal capacitance that varies with the applied voltage
explanation: A Zener diode operated in reverse breakdown holds a nearly constant voltage across it while the current through it varies widely. That makes it useful as a simple voltage reference or regulator.

question: What is the function of hysteresis in a comparator?
optionA: To prevent input noise from causing unstable output signals
optionB: To allow the comparator to be used with AC input signals
optionC: To cause the output to continually change states
explanation: Hysteresis sets two thresholds, one for rising and one for falling input. A noisy signal hovering near a single threshold would make the output chatter, but with hysteresis the output switches cleanly once and stays put.

question: What is piezoelectricity?
optionA: The ability of materials to generate electromagnetic waves of a certain frequency when voltage is applied
optionB: A characteristic of materials that have an index of refraction which depends on the polarization of the electromagnetic wave passing through it
optionC: A characteristic of materials that generate a voltage when stressed and that flex when a voltage is applied
optionD: The ability of materials to generate voltage when an electromagnetic wave of a certain frequency is applied
explanation: Piezoelectric materials such as quartz produce a voltage when mechanically stressed and bend or flex when a voltage is applied. This two-way effect is what lets a quartz crystal act as a stable resonator.

question: Why is gallium arsenide (GaAs) useful for semiconductor devices operating at UHF and higher frequencies?
optionC: Lower junction voltage drop
explanation: Gallium arsenide has much higher electron mobility than silicon, so carriers move faster, devices switch faster, and noise is lower at UHF and microwave frequencies. Higher noise figure would be a drawback, not a benefit.

question: What absorbs the energy from light falling on a photovoltaic cell?
optionC: Electrons
explanation: In a photovoltaic cell, electrons in the semiconductor absorb the energy of incoming light. Freed electrons and the holes they leave are swept apart by the junction field, producing current. Photons carry the energy; they are not what absorbs it.

question: Which of the following semiconductor materials contains excess free electrons?
optionC: Bipolar
explanation: N-type material is doped with donor atoms that have an extra valence electron, giving it excess free electrons as the majority carriers. P-type material instead has an excess of holes.

question: Which characteristic of a Schottky diode makes it a better choice than a silicon junction diode for use as a power supply rectifier?
optionC: Longer carrier retention time
explanation: A Schottky diode's metal-semiconductor junction has a forward drop of roughly 0.2 to 0.4 volts, compared with about 0.7 volts for silicon. Less drop means less wasted power and heat in a rectifier. Schottky diodes usually have lower, not higher, reverse breakdown.

question: What happens when the level of a comparator's input signal crosses the threshold voltage?
optionA: The IC input can be damaged
optionB: The comparator changes its output state
optionC: The reference level appears at the output
explanation: A comparator compares its input with a threshold. When the input crosses that threshold, the comparator switches its output from one state to the other, high to low or low to high.

question: What is the equivalent circuit of a quartz crystal?
optionA: Series RLC in parallel with a shunt C representing electrode and stray capacitance
optionB: Parallel RLC, where C is the parallel combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
optionC: Series RLC, where C is the parallel combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
optionD: Parallel RLC, where C is the series combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
explanation: A quartz crystal behaves like a series RLC circuit, representing its mechanical resonance, in parallel with a shunt capacitance from the electrodes, holder and strays. That gives it both a series and a slightly higher parallel resonant frequency.

question: Which of the following device packages is a through-hole type?
optionC: BGA
explanation: A DIP (dual in-line package) has two rows of pins that pass through holes in the circuit board, making it a through-hole package. PLCC, BGA and SOT packages are surface mount types.

question: What happens to photoconductive material when light shines on it?
optionC: Reflectivity increases
explanation: Light striking a photoconductive material frees additional charge carriers, so its resistance decreases. A photocell in a night light, for example, drops in resistance as the room gets brighter.

question: Why does a PN-junction diode not conduct current when reverse biased?
optionA: Only P-type semiconductor material can conduct current
optionB: Only N-type semiconductor material can conduct current
optionC: Holes in P-type material and electrons in the N-type material are separated by the applied voltage, widening the depletion region
optionD: Excess holes in P-type material combine with the electrons in N-type material, converting the entire diode into an insulator
explanation: Reverse bias pulls holes in the P side and electrons in the N side away from the junction. That widens the depletion region, which has almost no free carriers, so essentially no current crosses the junction.

question: What property of an LED's semiconductor material determines its forward voltage drop?
optionC: Junction capacitance
explanation: An LED's forward voltage is set by the band gap of its semiconductor, the energy an electron gives up when it crosses the junction. A wider band gap gives shorter wavelength light and a higher forward voltage, so blue LEDs need more volts than red ones.

question: What is tri-state logic?
optionA: Logic devices with 0, 1, and high-impedance output states
optionB: Logic devices that utilize ternary math
optionC: Logic with three output impedances which can be selected to better match the load impedance
explanation: Tri-state logic outputs can be a 0, a 1, or a third high-impedance state that effectively disconnects them. This lets several devices share one bus, with only the selected device driving it at a time.

question: Which of the following is an aspect of the piezoelectric effect?
optionA: Mechanical deformation of material due to the application of a voltage
optionB: Mechanical deformation of material due to the application of a magnetic field
optionC: Generation of electrical energy in the presence of light
optionD: Increased conductivity in the presence of light
explanation: One aspect of the piezoelectric effect is that applying a voltage mechanically deforms the material. The reverse also occurs, voltage from stress. Deformation from a magnetic field is magnetostriction, a different effect.

question: Which of the following materials supports the highest frequency of operation when used in MMICs?
optionC: Silicon dioxide
explanation: Gallium nitride has high electron velocity and a wide band gap, letting MMICs work at the highest frequencies and power levels listed. Silicon nitride and silicon dioxide are insulating layers, not active semiconductor material.

question: What is the most common configuration of an optoisolator or optocoupler?
optionC: An amplitude-modulated helium-neon laser
explanation: The usual optoisolator pairs an LED with a phototransistor in one sealed package. The LED's light switches the phototransistor, passing the signal across with no electrical connection between the two sides.

question: What is the name given to an impurity atom that adds holes to a semiconductor crystal structure?
optionC: Acceptor impurity
explanation: An acceptor impurity has one fewer valence electron than the semiconductor, so it accepts an electron and leaves a hole, making P-type material. A donor impurity does the opposite and adds free electrons.

question: What type of semiconductor device is designed for use as a voltage-controlled capacitor?
optionC: Silicon-controlled rectifier
explanation: A varactor diode is built so the width of its reverse-biased depletion region, and so its capacitance, changes with the applied voltage. It works as a voltage-controlled capacitor for tuning and frequency control.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of BiCMOS logic?
optionA: Its simplicity results in much less expensive devices than standard CMOS
optionB: It is immune to electrostatic damage
optionC: It has the high input impedance of CMOS and the low output impedance of bipolar transistors
explanation: BiCMOS combines CMOS transistors at the inputs, giving high input impedance and low drive current, with bipolar transistors at the outputs, giving low output impedance and strong drive. It is not immune to static and is generally more costly than plain CMOS.

question: Why are cores of inductors and transformers sometimes constructed of thin layers?
optionB: To reduce power loss from eddy currents in the core
optionC: To increase the cutoff frequency by reducing capacitance
optionD: To save cost by reducing the amount of magnetic material
explanation: A changing magnetic field induces circulating eddy currents in a conductive core, wasting power as heat. Building the core from thin insulated laminations breaks up those current paths and greatly reduces eddy current loss.

question: Which is the most common input and output impedance of MMICs?
optionC: 450 ohms
explanation: Most MMICs are designed with 50 ohm input and output impedance, so they drop straight into standard 50 ohm coax and microstrip systems without extra matching. 75 ohms is common in TV and video work, not typical MMICs.

question: What is the photovoltaic effect?
optionA: The conversion of voltage to current when exposed to light
optionB: The conversion of light to electrical energy
optionC: The effect that causes a photodiode to emit light when a voltage is applied
optionD: The effect that causes a phototransistor's beta to decrease when exposed to light
explanation: The photovoltaic effect is the direct conversion of light into electrical energy, the principle behind solar cells. A photodiode giving off light is the opposite process, which is what an LED does.

question: How does DC input impedance at the gate of a field-effect transistor (FET) compare with that of a bipolar transistor?
optionB: An FET has lower input impedance
optionC: An FET has higher input impedance
explanation: The gate of an FET is either a reverse-biased junction or insulated by oxide, so it draws almost no DC current and has very high input impedance. A bipolar transistor's base is forward biased and draws current, giving a much lower input impedance.

question: What characteristic of a PIN diode makes it useful as an RF switch?
optionB: Ability to dissipate large amounts of power
optionC: Reverse bias controls its forward voltage drop
explanation: A PIN diode has a wide intrinsic layer between its P and N regions, which gives it very low junction capacitance when reverse biased. That keeps RF from leaking through when the switch is off, while forward current lets RF pass when it is on.

question: Which of the following digital logic families has the lowest power consumption?
optionC: NMOS
explanation: CMOS logic draws almost no current except while switching, because one transistor of each complementary pair is always off. That gives it the lowest power consumption of these families. ECL is fast but draws considerable current all the time.

question: How do ferrite and powdered iron compare for use in an inductor core?
optionA: Ferrite cores generally have lower initial permeability
optionB: Ferrite cores generally have better temperature stability
optionC: Ferrite cores generally require fewer turns to produce a given inductance value
optionD: Ferrite cores are easier to use with surface-mount technology
explanation: Ferrite materials generally have higher permeability than powdered iron, so a ferrite core reaches a given inductance with fewer turns. Powdered iron usually wins on temperature stability, which is the tempting wrong choice.

question: Which of the following noise figure values is typical of a low-noise UHF preamplifier?
optionC: 44 dBm
explanation: Noise figure is a positive number in dB, and a good low-noise UHF preamplifier is around 0.5 dB, adding very little noise. A negative noise figure is not possible, and dBm is a unit of power, not noise figure.

question: Which of the following describes an optical shaft encoder?
optionA: A device that detects rotation by interrupting a light source with a patterned wheel
optionB: A device that measures the strength of a beam of light using analog-to-digital conversion
optionC: An optical computing device in which light is coupled between devices by fiber optics
optionD: A device for generating RTTY signals by means of a rotating light source
explanation: An optical shaft encoder detects rotation by shining a light through, or off, a wheel with a pattern of slots or marks. As the shaft turns, the interrupted light produces pulses that show position, direction or speed, as in a radio's tuning knob.

question: What is the beta of a bipolar junction transistor?
optionA: The frequency at which the current gain is reduced to 0.707
optionB: The change in collector current with respect to the change in base current
optionC: The breakdown voltage of the base-to-collector junction
explanation: Beta is the common-emitter current gain of a bipolar transistor, the change in collector current divided by the change in base current. A transistor with a beta of 100 changes collector current 100 times as much as base current.

question: Which of the following is a common use of a Schottky diode?
optionA: In oscillator circuits as the negative resistance element
optionB: As a variable capacitance in an automatic frequency control circuit
optionC: In power supplies as a constant voltage reference
optionD: As a VHF/UHF mixer or detector
explanation: Schottky diodes have very little stored charge, so they switch extremely fast, which suits them to VHF and UHF mixers and detectors. Negative resistance oscillators use tunnel diodes, and voltage references use Zener diodes.

question: Why do CMOS digital integrated circuits have high immunity to noise on the input signal or power supply?
optionB: The input switching threshold is about twice the power supply voltage
optionC: The input switching threshold is about half the power supply voltage
explanation: A CMOS input switches at roughly half the supply voltage, leaving wide margins on both sides. Noise has to move the input nearly halfway across the supply range before it causes a false state change.

question: What core material property determines the inductance of an inductor?
optionC: Reactivity
explanation: Inductance depends on the core's permeability, how easily it supports a magnetic field. Higher permeability gives more inductance for the same coil. Permittivity is the electric field property that matters for capacitors.

question: What characteristics of MMICs make them a popular choice for VHF through microwave circuits?
optionA: The ability to retrieve information from a single signal, even in the presence of other strong signals
optionB: Extremely high Q factor and high stability over a wide temperature range
optionC: Nearly infinite gain, very high input impedance, and very low output impedance
optionD: Controlled gain, low noise figure, and constant input and output impedance over the specified frequency range
explanation: MMICs offer a set amount of gain, a low noise figure, and steady input and output impedance, usually 50 ohms, across a wide frequency range. That makes them easy building blocks from VHF to microwave. Near-infinite gain and very high input impedance describe an op amp.

question: Which of these materials is most commonly used to create photoconductive devices?
optionC: Crystalline semiconductor
explanation: Photoconductive devices are most commonly made from crystalline semiconductor material, whose resistance falls when light frees charge carriers. Argon is an inert gas and the other listed material is not a photoconductor.

question: Which of the following indicates that a silicon NPN junction transistor is biased on?
optionA: Base-to-emitter resistance of approximately 6 ohms to 7 ohms
optionB: Base-to-emitter resistance of approximately 0.6 ohms to 0.7 ohms
optionC: Base-to-emitter voltage of approximately 6 volts to 7 volts
optionD: Base-to-emitter voltage of approximately 0.6 volts to 0.7 volts
explanation: A silicon base-emitter junction starts conducting at about 0.6 to 0.7 volts forward bias, so that voltage shows the transistor is turned on. Six or seven volts would exceed the reverse breakdown of many junctions and is not a normal on condition.

question: What causes a junction diode to fail from excessive current?
optionC: Insufficient forward voltage
explanation: Current through a diode's forward drop produces heat. Too much current raises the junction temperature past its limit and the junction is damaged. Excessive inverse voltage is a different failure, one caused by voltage rather than current.

question: What best describes a pull-up or pull-down resistor?
optionA: A resistor in a keying circuit used to reduce key clicks
optionB: A resistor connected to the positive or negative supply used to establish a voltage when an input or output is an open circuit
optionC: A resistor that ensures that an oscillator frequency does not drift
optionD: A resistor connected to an op-amp output that prevents signals from exceeding the power supply voltage
explanation: A pull-up or pull-down resistor ties a line to the positive supply or to ground so it sits at a known logic level when nothing is driving it, such as an open switch or a tri-state output. Without it the input could float and read randomly.

question: Which of the following materials has the highest temperature stability of its magnetic characteristics?
optionC: Ferrite
explanation: Powdered iron cores keep their magnetic characteristics more stable over temperature than ferrite, which is why they are favored for tuned circuits and oscillators. Brass and aluminum are not magnetic core materials at all.

question: What type of transmission line is often used for connections to MMICs?
optionC: Parallel wire
explanation: MMICs are usually mounted on circuit boards with microstrip lines, a trace over a ground plane with a controlled impedance such as 50 ohms. Microstrip is easy to build on a board and suits the small size of these devices.

question: What is a solid-state relay?
optionA: A relay that uses transistors to drive the relay coil
optionB: A device that uses semiconductors to implement the functions of an electromechanical relay
optionC: A mechanical relay that latches in the on or off state each time it is pulsed
optionD: A semiconductor switch that uses a monostable multivibrator circuit
explanation: A solid-state relay uses semiconductors, such as an optoisolator driving a triac or MOSFET, to do the job of an electromechanical relay with no moving contacts. A transistor driving a mechanical relay coil is still a mechanical relay.

question: What is the term for the frequency at which the grounded-base current gain of a bipolar junction transistor has decreased to 0.7 of the gain obtainable at 1 kHz?
optionC: Beta cutoff frequency
explanation: Alpha is the common (grounded) base current gain. The frequency where alpha falls to about 0.707 of its low-frequency value is the alpha cutoff frequency. Beta cutoff is the matching term for the common-emitter gain.

question: Which of the following is a Schottky barrier diode?
optionC: PIN junction
explanation: A Schottky barrier diode is formed by a junction of metal against a semiconductor, rather than a PN junction. That structure gives its low forward voltage and fast switching. A PIN junction describes a different diode type.

question: What is used to design the configuration of a field-programmable gate array (FPGA)?
optionC: An auto-router
explanation: An FPGA's internal logic is described in a hardware description language such as VHDL or Verilog, then compiled into a configuration file loaded into the chip. Karnaugh maps help simplify small logic expressions but do not configure an FPGA.

question: What devices are commonly used as VHF and UHF parasitic suppressors at the input and output terminals of a transistor HF amplifier?
optionC: Ferrite beads
explanation: A ferrite bead slipped over a lead adds loss at VHF and UHF while having little effect at HF. Placed at a transistor amplifier's input and output, it damps unwanted high-frequency parasitic oscillations.

question: How is power supplied to the most common type of MMIC?
optionA: Through a capacitor and RF choke connected to the amplifier input lead
optionC: Through a resistor and/or RF choke connected to the amplifier output lead
optionD: Directly to the bias voltage (Vcc) lead
explanation: The common MMIC has no separate bias pin. DC is fed to the output lead through a resistor, an RF choke or both, which deliver supply current while keeping the RF signal from leaking into the power supply.

question: Why are optoisolators often used in conjunction with solid-state circuits that control 120 VAC circuits?
optionA: Optoisolators provide a low-impedance link between a control circuit and a power circuit
optionB: Optoisolators provide impedance matching between the control circuit and power circuit
optionC: Optoisolators provide an electrical isolation between a control circuit and the circuit being switched
optionD: Optoisolators eliminate the effects of reflected light in the control circuit
explanation: An optoisolator passes the control signal as light, so there is no electrical path between the low-voltage control circuit and the 120 VAC circuit it switches. That isolation protects the control circuit and the user from line voltage.

question: What is a depletion-mode field-effect transistor (FET)?
optionA: An FET that exhibits a current flow between source and drain when no gate voltage is applied
optionB: An FET that has no current flow between source and drain when no gate voltage is applied
optionC: An FET that exhibits very high electron mobility due to a lack of holes in the N-type material
optionD: An FET for which holes are the majority carriers
explanation: A depletion-mode FET already has a conducting channel, so current flows from source to drain with zero gate voltage. Gate voltage of the proper polarity depletes the channel and reduces current. An enhancement-mode FET is off at zero gate voltage.

question: What is a common use for point-contact diodes?
optionC: As an RF detector
explanation: A point-contact diode uses a fine wire touching a semiconductor, giving very low capacitance. That makes it well suited to detecting RF signals, as in crystal radio receivers and RF probes, rather than handling power.

question: What is a primary advantage of using a toroidal core instead of a solenoidal core in an inductor?
optionA: Toroidal cores confine most of the magnetic field within the core material
optionB: Toroidal cores make it easier to couple the magnetic energy into other components
optionC: Toroidal cores exhibit greater hysteresis
optionD: Toroidal cores have lower Q characteristics
