explanation: A toroid is a closed ring, so most of the magnetic field stays inside the core. That reduces coupling to nearby parts and means the coil can be mounted close to other components. Coupling more energy to other parts is the opposite of its advantage.

question: Which of the following component package types have the least parasitic effects at frequencies above the HF range?
optionC: Radial lead
explanation: Surface mount parts have no long leads, so they add the least stray inductance and capacitance above HF. TO-220, axial and radial lead packages all have leads that add parasitic reactance at VHF and higher.

question: What is the efficiency of a photovoltaic cell?
optionA: The output RF power divided by the input DC power
optionB: The output in lumens divided by the input power in watts
optionC: The open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current under full illumination
optionD: The relative fraction of light that is converted to current
explanation: Efficiency of a photovoltaic cell is the fraction of the incoming light energy that it converts into electrical output. Ratios of RF power, lumens or voltage to current describe other things entirely.

question: What is the purpose of connecting Zener diodes between a MOSFET gate and its source or drain?
optionA: To provide a voltage reference for the correct amount of reverse-bias gate voltage
optionB: To protect the substrate from excessive voltages
optionC: To keep the gate voltage within specifications and prevent the device from overheating
optionD: To protect the gate from static damage
explanation: A MOSFET gate is insulated by a very thin oxide layer that static discharge can puncture. Zener diodes from gate to source or drain clamp any voltage spike before it reaches that layer, protecting the gate from static damage.

question: What is used to control the attenuation of RF signals by a PIN diode?
optionC: Reverse voltage larger than the RF signal
optionD: Capacitance of an RF coupling capacitor
explanation: The RF resistance of a PIN diode falls as its forward DC bias current rises. Varying that DC current therefore varies how much RF the diode passes or shunts, making it a current-controlled RF attenuator.

question: Which type of core material decreases inductance when inserted into a coil?
optionC: Ferrite
explanation: Brass is a nonmagnetic conductor. A changing field induces eddy currents in a brass slug that oppose the coil's field, so inserting it lowers inductance. Ferrite raises inductance because of its high permeability.

question: What advantage does surface-mount technology offer at RF compared to using through-hole components?
optionC: Components have less parasitic inductance and capacitance
explanation: Surface mount technology offers all of these advantages: smaller circuit area, shorter board traces, and less parasitic inductance and capacitance because the parts have little or no leads. Together these improve RF performance.

question: What is the most common material used in power-generating photovoltaic cells?
optionC: Cadmium sulfide
explanation: Silicon is by far the most common material in power-generating solar cells because it is plentiful, well understood and reasonably efficient. Selenium and cadmium sulfide appear in older or light-sensing devices.

question: What causes inductor saturation?
optionA: Operation at too high a frequency
optionB: Selecting a core with low permeability
optionC: Operation at excessive magnetic flux
optionD: Selecting a core with excessive permittivity
explanation: A core saturates when the magnetic flux, from too much current, reaches the most the material can carry. Beyond that, more current produces little more flux, permeability drops, and inductance falls sharply.

question: What is a characteristic of DIP packaging used for integrated circuits?
optionA: Extremely low stray capacitance (dielectrically isolated package)
optionB: Extremely high resistance between pins (doubly insulated package)
optionC: Two chips in each package (dual in package)
optionD: Two rows of connecting pins on opposite sides of package (dual in-line package)
explanation: DIP stands for dual in-line package, an IC case with two parallel rows of pins on opposite sides. The other expansions given are made up and do not describe the package.

question: What is the approximate open-circuit voltage produced by a fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell?
optionC: 1.1 volts
explanation: A single fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell produces about 0.5 volts open circuit, so solar panels connect many cells in series to reach useful voltages. The 0.7 volt figure is the forward drop of a silicon diode, the tempting mix-up.

question: Why are DIP through-hole package ICs not typically used at UHF and higher frequencies?
optionB: Epoxy coating is conductive above 300 MHz
optionC: Excessive lead length
optionD: Unsuitable for combining analog and digital signals
explanation: The pins of a DIP package and its internal bond wires are relatively long, and at UHF and above that lead length adds significant inductance and capacitance. Excessive lead length, not the epoxy or dielectric, is what rules it out.

question: Which circuit is bistable?
optionC: A flip-flop
explanation: A flip-flop has two stable states and stays in whichever one it was last set to until a new input changes it, so it is bistable. AND and OR gates simply follow their inputs and hold no state of their own.

question: For what portion of the signal cycle does each active element in a push-pull, Class AB amplifier conduct?
optionA: More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees
optionC: The entire cycle
explanation: Class AB bias sits between Class B and Class A, so each device conducts a little longer than half the cycle but not all of it: more than 180 but less than 360 degrees. The overlap reduces crossover distortion compared to Class B.

question: How are the capacitors and inductors of a low-pass filter Pi-network arranged between the network's input and output?
optionA: Two inductors are in series between the input and output, and a capacitor is connected between the two inductors and ground
optionB: Two capacitors are in series between the input and output, and an inductor is connected between the two capacitors and ground
optionC: An inductor is connected between the input and ground, another inductor is connected between the output and ground, and a capacitor is connected between the input and output
optionD: A capacitor is connected between the input and ground, another capacitor is connected between the output and ground, and an inductor is connected between the input and output
explanation: A low-pass Pi-network looks like the Greek letter pi: a capacitor from the input to ground, a second capacitor from the output to ground, and a series inductor bridging them. Series inductance and shunt capacitance both block higher frequencies.

question: How does a linear electronic voltage regulator work?
optionA: It has a ramp voltage as its output
optionB: It eliminates the need for a pass transistor
optionC: The control element duty cycle is proportional to the line or load conditions
optionD: The conduction of a control element is varied to maintain a constant output voltage
explanation: A linear regulator compares the output to a reference and continuously adjusts how much a pass element conducts, acting like a variable resistor, to hold the output voltage constant. Changing a duty cycle is how a switching regulator works instead.

question: Which of the following can be used to generate FM phone signals?
optionA: Balanced modulation of the audio amplifier
optionB: Reactance modulation of a local oscillator
optionC: Reactance modulation of the final amplifier
optionD: Balanced modulation of a local oscillator
explanation: A reactance modulator varies the capacitance in an oscillator's tuning circuit with the audio, shifting its frequency to produce FM or PM. It is applied to a low-level local oscillator, not the final amplifier, and later stages multiply the deviation.

question: What is meant by "direct sampling" in software defined radios?
optionA: Software is converted from source code to object code during operation of the receiver
optionB: I and Q signals are generated by digital processing without the use of RF amplification
optionC: Incoming RF is digitized by an analog-to-digital converter without being mixed with a local oscillator signal
optionD: A switching mixer is used to generate I and Q signals directly from the RF input
explanation: In a direct-sampling SDR, a fast analog-to-digital converter digitizes the RF signal straight from the antenna, often after filtering and amplification, with no analog mixing against a local oscillator. All tuning and demodulation then happen in software.

question: What is the typical output impedance of an op-amp?
optionC: 100 ohms
explanation: An op-amp's output impedance is very low, close to zero ohms in the ideal case, especially with negative feedback applied. That lets it drive loads without its output voltage sagging.

question: What are three common oscillator circuits?
optionC: Taft, Hartley, and Pierce
explanation: The Colpitts, Hartley and Pierce circuits are three classic oscillator types. Colpitts uses a capacitive divider for feedback, Hartley a tapped coil, and Pierce a quartz crystal. Taft, Fenner and Beane are not oscillator circuits.

question: What is the function of a decade counter?
optionA: It produces one output pulse for every 10 input pulses
optionB: It decodes a decimal number for display on a seven-segment LED display
optionC: It produces 10 output pulses for every input pulse
optionD: It decodes a binary number for display on a seven-segment LED display
explanation: A decade counter counts ten input pulses and then resets, giving one output pulse for every ten in, so it divides by 10. Decoding numbers for a seven-segment display is the job of a separate decoder chip.

question: What is a Class D amplifier?
optionA: An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency
optionB: A low power amplifier that uses a differential amplifier for improved linearity
optionC: An amplifier that uses drift-mode FETs for high efficiency
optionD: An amplifier biased to be relatively free from distortion
explanation: A Class D amplifier drives its output devices as switches, fully on or fully off, using pulse width modulation or similar methods. Little power is lost in a device that is saturated or cut off, so efficiency is high.

question: What is the frequency response of a T-network with series capacitors and a shunt inductor?
optionC: Band-pass
explanation: Series capacitors pass high frequencies and block low ones, and a shunt inductor shorts low frequencies to ground. Both act together to make the T-network a high-pass filter.

question: How does a switchmode voltage regulator work?
optionA: By alternating the output between positive and negative voltages
optionB: By varying the duty cycle of pulses input to a filter
optionC: By varying the conductivity of a pass element
optionD: By switching between two Zener diode reference voltages
explanation: A switchmode regulator turns a switch on and off and sends the pulses through an LC filter that averages them. Changing the duty cycle, the fraction of time the switch is on, sets the output voltage.

question: What is the function of a reactance modulator?
optionA: Produce PM or FM signals by varying a resistance
optionB: Produce AM signals by varying an inductance
optionC: Produce AM signals by varying a resistance
optionD: Produce PM or FM signals by varying a capacitance
explanation: A reactance modulator, often a varactor or a transistor acting as a variable capacitance, changes the effective capacitance in an oscillator's tuned circuit in step with the audio. That shifts frequency or phase, producing FM or PM rather than AM.

question: What kind of digital signal processing audio filter is used to remove unwanted noise from a received SSB signal?
optionC: A Hilbert-transform filter
explanation: An adaptive filter continually adjusts its coefficients to tell the random noise apart from the correlated speech and suppress the noise. A Hilbert-transform filter is used to create SSB, not to clean up received noise.

question: What is the frequency response of the circuit in E7-3 if a capacitor is added across the feedback resistor?
optionC: Band-pass filter
explanation: A capacitor across the feedback resistor lowers the feedback impedance as frequency rises, which reduces the stage gain at higher frequencies. Low frequencies still see the full resistor, so the circuit becomes a low-pass filter.

question: What is a microphonic?
optionA: An IC used for amplifying microphone signals
optionB: Distortion caused by RF pickup on the microphone cable
optionC: Changes in oscillator frequency caused by mechanical vibration
optionD: Excess loading of the microphone by an oscillator
explanation: A microphonic is an unwanted frequency change in an oscillator caused by mechanical vibration or shock, which physically moves its components and shifts their inductance or capacitance. It can show up as a warble on the signal.

question: Which of the following can divide the frequency of a pulse train by 2?
optionC: An OR gate
explanation: A toggle-wired flip-flop changes state once per input pulse, so its output completes one full cycle for every two input pulses, halving the frequency. An XOR or OR gate has no memory and cannot count pulses.

question: What circuit is required at the output of an RF switching amplifier?
optionA: A filter to remove harmonic content
optionB: A high-pass filter to compensate for low gain at low frequencies
optionC: A matched load resistor to prevent damage by switching transients
optionD: A temperature compensating load resistor to improve linearity
explanation: A switching amplifier's output is close to a square wave, which is rich in harmonics. A low-pass or band-pass filter at the output removes that harmonic content so only the wanted frequency reaches the antenna.

question: What is the purpose of adding an inductor to a Pi-network to create a Pi-L-network?
optionC: To eliminate one capacitor
explanation: A Pi-L network adds a series output inductor after the Pi-network, forming a second low-pass section. That extra section gives greater attenuation of harmonics than a plain Pi-network.

question: What device is used as a stable voltage reference?
optionC: An SCR
explanation: A Zener diode held in reverse breakdown keeps a nearly constant voltage across itself over a wide range of current, so it makes a simple, stable voltage reference. An SCR is a switching device, not a reference.

question: What is a frequency discriminator?
optionB: A circuit for filtering closely adjacent signals
optionC: An automatic band-switching circuit
optionD: A circuit for detecting FM signals
explanation: A frequency discriminator is an FM detector: it turns changes in the frequency of the incoming signal into changes in output voltage, recovering the audio. It does not generate FM or filter adjacent signals.

question: What type of digital signal processing filter is used to generate an SSB signal?
optionC: A Hilbert-transform filter
explanation: A Hilbert-transform filter shifts every frequency component by 90 degrees. Combining the shifted and unshifted signals lets the DSP cancel one sideband and keep the other, the digital version of the phasing method.

question: What is the typical input impedance of an op-amp?
optionC: Very low
explanation: An op-amp's input impedance is very high, ideally infinite, so it draws almost no current from the signal source. Low input impedance would load down the previous stage.

question: What is a phase-locked loop?
optionA: An electronic servo loop consisting of a ratio detector, reactance modulator, and voltage-controlled oscillator
optionB: An electronic circuit also known as a monostable multivibrator
optionC: An electronic servo loop consisting of a phase detector, a low-pass filter, a voltage-controlled oscillator, and a stable reference oscillator
optionD: An electronic circuit consisting of a precision push-pull amplifier with a differential phase input
explanation: A phase-locked loop is a servo loop. A phase detector compares a voltage-controlled oscillator with a stable reference, and a low-pass filter turns the error into a control voltage that keeps the VCO locked in phase.

question: How many flip-flops are required to divide a signal frequency by 16?
explanation: Each flip-flop divides by 2, so n stages divide by 2 to the power n. For 16: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16, which takes 4 flip-flops. Using 16 flip-flops would divide by 2^16 = 65,536.

question: What is the operating point of a Class A common emitter amplifier?
optionA: Approximately halfway between saturation and cutoff
optionB: Approximately halfway between the emitter voltage and the base voltage
optionC: At a point where the bias resistor equals the load resistor
optionD: At a point where the load line intersects the zero bias current curve
explanation: For Class A, the transistor is biased about halfway between saturation and cutoff so the signal can swing equally up and down without clipping. The device conducts for the full 360 degrees of the cycle.

question: How does an impedance-matching circuit transform a complex impedance to a resistive impedance?
optionA: It introduces negative resistance to cancel the resistive part of impedance
optionB: It introduces transconductance to cancel the reactive part of impedance
optionC: It cancels the reactive part of the impedance and changes the resistive part to the desired value
optionD: Reactive currents are dissipated in matched resistances
explanation: A matching network adds reactance of the opposite sign to cancel the load's reactive part, and it transforms the remaining resistance up or down to the value the source wants, such as 50 ohms.

question: Which of the following describes a three-terminal voltage regulator?
optionC: A shunt regulator
explanation: A common three-terminal regulator such as the 78xx series is a series regulator: input, output and ground, with an internal pass transistor in series with the load. It contains the reference, error amplifier and protection in one package.

question: What is one way to produce a single-sideband phone signal?
optionA: Use a balanced modulator followed by a filter
optionB: Use a reactance modulator followed by a mixer
optionC: Use a loop modulator followed by a mixer
optionD: Use a product detector with a DSB signal
explanation: A balanced modulator produces both sidebands and suppresses the carrier, giving double sideband. A sharp filter then removes one sideband, leaving single sideband. This is the classic filter method.

question: Which method generates an SSB signal using digital signal processing?
optionA: Mixing products are converted to voltages and subtracted by adder circuits
optionB: A frequency synthesizer removes unwanted sidebands
optionC: Varying quartz crystal characteristics are emulated in digital form
optionD: Signals are combined in quadrature phase relationship
explanation: The DSP creates I and Q versions of the audio that are 90 degrees apart and combines them in quadrature with carrier signals that are also 90 degrees apart. One sideband adds and the other cancels, leaving SSB.

question: What is meant by the term "op-amp input offset voltage"?
optionA: The output voltage of the op-amp minus its input voltage
optionB: The difference between the output voltage of the op-amp and the input voltage required in the immediately following stage
optionC: The differential input voltage needed to bring the open loop output voltage to zero
optionD: The potential between the amplifier input terminals of the op-amp in an open loop condition
explanation: Input offset voltage is the small DC voltage that must be applied between the two inputs to bring the open-loop output to zero. It exists because the input transistors are never perfectly matched.

question: How is positive feedback supplied in a Colpitts oscillator?
optionC: Through a capacitive divider
explanation: A Colpitts oscillator takes its positive feedback from a capacitive voltage divider, two capacitors in series across the tank circuit. A tapped coil is the feedback method of the Hartley oscillator.

question: Which of the following circuits continuously alternates between two states without an external clock signal?
optionC: T flip-flop
explanation: An astable multivibrator has no stable state, so it keeps flipping between its two states on its own and works as a free-running square wave oscillator. A monostable needs a trigger, and J-K and T flip-flops need a clock or input.

question: What can be done to prevent unwanted oscillations in an RF power amplifier?
optionA: Tune the stage for minimum loading
optionB: Tune both the input and output for maximum power
optionC: Install parasitic suppressors and/or neutralize the stage
optionD: Use a phase inverter in the output filter
explanation: Parasitic suppressors damp unwanted VHF oscillations in the leads and tube or transistor circuit, and neutralization cancels the internal feedback capacitance that can make a stage oscillate. Tuning for maximum power alone does not stop either.

question: Which filter type has ripple in the passband and a sharp cutoff?
optionC: A passive op-amp filter
explanation: A Chebyshev filter trades a small, controlled ripple in the passband for a steeper cutoff than a Butterworth filter of the same order. A Butterworth filter is maximally flat in the passband with a gentler rolloff.

question: Which of the following types of linear voltage regulator operates by loading the unregulated voltage source?
optionC: A shunt current source
explanation: A shunt regulator sits in parallel with the load and draws whatever current is needed to drop the excess voltage across a series resistor, so it loads the unregulated source. A series regulator instead controls current flowing through to the load.

question: What is added to an FM speech channel to boost the higher audio frequencies?
optionC: A heterodyne enhancer
explanation: A pre-emphasis network in the transmitter boosts higher audio frequencies before modulation, improving their signal-to-noise ratio. The receiver's de-emphasis network then cuts them back to restore a flat response.

question: How frequently must an analog signal be sampled to be accurately reproduced?
optionA: At least half the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
optionB: At least twice the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
optionC: At the same rate as the highest frequency component of the signal
optionD: At four times the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
explanation: By the Nyquist rule, the sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal. For audio up to 3 kHz that means at least 6,000 samples per second. Sampling slower causes aliasing.

question: How can unwanted ringing and audio instability be prevented in an op-amp audio filter?
optionC: Restrict Q but increase gain
explanation: High gain and high Q both make an active filter more prone to ringing and instability. Keeping both gain and Q modest gives a stable filter that does not ring on transients.

question: How is positive feedback supplied in a Pierce oscillator?
optionC: Through a neutralizing capacitor
explanation: In a Pierce oscillator the quartz crystal sits in the feedback path and supplies the positive feedback at its resonant frequency. That gives the Pierce oscillator excellent frequency stability.

question: What is a characteristic of a monostable multivibrator?
optionA: It switches temporarily to an alternate state for a set time
optionB: It produces a continuous square wave
optionC: It stores one bit of data
optionD: It maintains a constant output voltage, regardless of variations in the input voltage
explanation: A monostable multivibrator rests in one stable state. A trigger pushes it into its other state for a time set by an RC network, then it returns on its own. That is why it is called a one-shot.

question: What is a characteristic of a grounded-grid amplifier?
optionC: High electrostatic damage protection
explanation: In a grounded-grid amplifier the drive is applied to the cathode, which presents a low input impedance, often around 50 to 100 ohms. The grid shields input from output, so neutralizing is rarely needed, but power gain is modest.

question: What are the characteristics of an elliptical filter?
optionA: Gradual passband rolloff with minimal stop-band ripple
optionB: Extremely flat response over its pass band with gradually rounded stop-band corners
optionC: Extremely sharp cutoff with one or more notches in the stop band
optionD: Gradual passband rolloff with extreme stop-band ripple
explanation: An elliptical (Cauer) filter places one or more zeros, or notches, in the stop band, which gives it an extremely sharp transition from pass to stop. The cost is ripple in both the passband and the stop band.

question: How is battery operating time calculated?
optionA: Average current divided by capacity in amp-hours
optionB: Average current divided by internal resistance
optionC: Capacity in amp-hours divided by average current
optionD: Internal resistance divided by average current
explanation: Operating time equals capacity divided by average current. For example, a 10 amp-hour battery supplying an average of 2 amps lasts about 10 / 2 = 5 hours. Dividing current by capacity gives an inverted, meaningless result.

question: Why is de-emphasis used in FM communications receivers?
optionA: For compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation
optionC: For higher efficiency
explanation: Phase modulation inherently gives more deviation to higher audio frequencies, which acts like pre-emphasis. De-emphasis in the receiver rolls those highs back off, so an FM receiver sounds correct on PM transmitters.

question: What is the minimum number of bits required to sample a signal with a range of 1 volt at a resolution of 1 millivolt?
optionC: 8 bits
explanation: Levels needed = 1 V / 0.001 V = 1,000. Nine bits give 2^9 = 512 levels, which is too few, while 10 bits give 2^10 = 1,024 levels, so 10 bits is the minimum. Eight bits give only 256 levels.

question: What is the gain-bandwidth of an operational amplifier?
optionA: The maximum frequency for a filter circuit using that type of amplifier
optionB: The frequency at which the open-loop gain of the amplifier equals one
optionC: The gain of the amplifier at a filter's cutoff frequency
optionD: The frequency at which the amplifier's offset voltage is zero
explanation: Gain-bandwidth is the frequency at which the op-amp's open-loop gain falls to one. Gain times bandwidth stays about constant, so a part with a 1 MHz figure set for a gain of 10 has roughly 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz of bandwidth.

question: Which of these functions can be performed by a phase-locked loop?
optionA: Wide-band AF and RF power amplification
optionC: Photovoltaic conversion and optical coupling
optionD: Comparison of two digital input signals and digital pulse counting
explanation: A phase-locked loop can generate many stable frequencies from one reference by dividing the VCO output in the loop, which is frequency synthesis. Its control voltage tracks an incoming FM signal, so it can demodulate FM too.

question: What logical operation does a NAND gate perform?
optionA: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 0
optionB: It produces a 1 at its output only if all inputs are 1
optionC: It produces a 0 at its output if some but not all inputs are 1
optionD: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 1
explanation: NAND is an AND gate with its output inverted. AND gives a 1 only when every input is 1, so NAND gives a 0 only in that case and a 1 for every other input combination.

question: Which of the following is the likely result of using a Class C amplifier to amplify a single-sideband phone signal?
optionC: Reduced third-order intermodulation
explanation: SSB is an amplitude-varying signal, so it needs a linear amplifier. A Class C stage is very nonlinear, which flattens and distorts the envelope and creates intermodulation products that spread the signal over excessive bandwidth.

question: Which describes a Pi-L network?
optionB: A Pi-network with an additional output series inductor
optionC: A network with only three discrete parts
optionD: A matching network in which all components are isolated from ground
explanation: A Pi-L network is an ordinary Pi-network followed by an additional series inductor at the output. The added inductor adds harmonic suppression and helps match higher or lower load impedances.

question: Why is a switching type power supply less expensive and lighter than an equivalent linear power supply?
optionA: The inverter design does not require an output filter circuit
optionB: The control circuitry uses less current, therefore smaller heat sinks are required
optionC: The high frequency inverter design uses much smaller transformers and filter components for an equivalent power output
optionD: It recovers power from the unused portion of the AC cycle, thus using fewer components
explanation: A switching supply runs its transformer at tens or hundreds of kilohertz instead of 60 Hz. Transformer core size and filter capacitance needed shrink as frequency rises, so the parts are much smaller, lighter and cheaper.

question: What is meant by the term "baseband" in radio communications?
optionA: The lowest frequency band that the transmitter or receiver covers
optionB: The frequency range occupied by a message signal prior to modulation
optionC: The unmodulated bandwidth of the transmitted signal
optionD: The basic oscillator frequency in an FM transmitter that is multiplied to increase the deviation and carrier frequency
explanation: Baseband is the frequency range of the message signal itself before it modulates a carrier, such as the audio from a microphone or a data stream. It is not the lowest band a transceiver covers.

question: What function is performed by a Fast Fourier Transform?
optionA: Converting analog signals to digital form
optionB: Converting digital signals to analog form
optionC: Converting signals from the time domain to the frequency domain
optionD: Converting signals from the frequency domain to the time domain
explanation: A Fast Fourier Transform is an efficient algorithm that takes a block of time-domain samples and computes the frequency content, the basis of an SDR waterfall or spectrum display. The inverse FFT goes the other direction.

question: How does the gain of an ideal operational amplifier vary with frequency?
optionA: It increases linearly with increasing frequency
optionB: It decreases linearly with increasing frequency
optionC: It decreases logarithmically with increasing frequency
optionD: It does not vary with frequency
explanation: An ideal op-amp is defined to have infinite gain at every frequency, so its gain does not vary with frequency. Real op-amps lose gain as frequency rises, but the ideal model ignores that.

question: How can an oscillator's microphonic responses be reduced?
optionB: Reduce noise on the oscillator's power supply
optionC: Increase the gain
optionD: Mechanically isolate the oscillator circuitry from its enclosure
explanation: Because vibration moves parts and shifts the frequency, the fix is to mechanically isolate the oscillator, for example with shock mounts or by keeping it rigid and apart from a vibrating enclosure. NP0 capacitors address temperature drift instead.

question: What logical operation does an OR gate perform?
optionA: It produces a 1 at its output if any input is 1
optionB: It produces a 0 at its output if all inputs are 1
optionC: It produces a 0 at its output if some but not all inputs are 1
optionD: It produces a 1 at its output if all inputs are 0
explanation: An OR gate outputs 1 whenever at least one input is 1, and outputs 0 only when every input is 0. Requiring all inputs to be 1 would describe an AND gate instead.

question: Why are switching amplifiers more efficient than linear amplifiers?
optionA: Switching amplifiers operate at higher voltages
optionB: The switching device is at saturation or cutoff most of the time
optionC: Linear amplifiers have high gain resulting in higher harmonic content
explanation: A switching device wastes little power when fully on (high current but nearly no voltage across it) or fully off (voltage but nearly no current). Since it spends most of its time in saturation or cutoff, losses stay low.

question: Which of the following is most frequently used as a band-pass or notch filter in VHF and UHF transceivers?
optionC: A swinging choke filter
explanation: A helical filter uses coils inside shielded cavities to form high-Q resonators in a small space, which makes it a common band-pass or notch filter at VHF and UHF. Sallen-Key filters are active audio-range designs.

question: What is the purpose of an inverter connected to a solar panel output?
optionA: Reduce AC ripple on the output
optionB: Maintain voltage with varying illumination levels
optionC: Prevent discharge when panel is not illuminated
optionD: Convert the panel's output from DC to AC
explanation: Solar panels produce direct current. An inverter converts that DC into AC so it can run ordinary household equipment or feed the power grid. Preventing nighttime discharge is the job of a blocking diode, not an inverter.

question: What are the principal frequencies that appear at the output of a mixer?
optionA: Two and four times the input frequency
optionB: The square root of the product of input frequencies
optionC: The two input frequencies along with their sum and difference frequencies
explanation: A mixer outputs the two original frequencies plus their sum and their difference. Example: mixing 10 MHz and 1 MHz gives 10, 1, 11 and 9 MHz, and a filter selects the wanted product.

question: What is the function of decimation?
optionA: Converting data to binary-coded decimal form
optionB: Reducing the effective sample rate by removing samples
optionC: Attenuating the signal
explanation: Decimation lowers the sample rate by keeping only every Nth sample and discarding the rest, which reduces the processing load. It must be preceded by low-pass filtering to avoid aliasing.

question: What is an operational amplifier?
optionA: A high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance
optionB: A digital audio amplifier whose characteristics are determined by components external to the amplifier
optionC: An amplifier used to increase the average output of frequency modulated amateur signals to the legal limit
optionD: A RF amplifier used in the UHF and microwave regions
explanation: An operational amplifier is a high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance. External feedback components set its actual circuit gain and response.

question: Which of the following components can be used to reduce thermal drift in crystal oscillators?
optionC: Wirewound resistors
explanation: NP0 (also called C0G) capacitors have a near-zero temperature coefficient, so their value barely changes as they warm up. Using them in an oscillator's tuning reduces thermal drift.

question: What logical operation is performed by a two-input exclusive NOR gate?
optionA: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 0
optionB: It produces a 1 at its output only if all inputs are 1
optionC: It produces a 0 at its output if one and only one of its inputs is 1
optionD: It produces a 1 at its output if one and only one input is 1
explanation: An exclusive OR gives 1 when exactly one input is 1. The exclusive NOR inverts that, so it gives 0 when one and only one input is 1 and gives 1 when both inputs match. It works as an equality detector.

question: What is characteristic of an emitter follower (or common collector) amplifier?
optionA: Low input impedance and phase inversion from input to output
optionC: Acts as an OR circuit if one input is grounded
explanation: An emitter follower has high input impedance, low output impedance and voltage gain just under one, with the output in phase with the input. Phase inversion belongs to the common emitter configuration, not this one.

question: What is a crystal lattice filter?
optionA: A power supply filter made with interlaced quartz crystals
optionB: An audio filter made with four quartz crystals that resonate at 1 kHz intervals
optionC: A filter using lattice-shaped quartz crystals for high-Q performance
optionD: A filter for low-level signals made using quartz crystals
explanation: A crystal lattice filter is built from quartz crystals, usually in matched pairs, arranged to give a narrow, steep-sided passband for low-level signals such as an IF stage. The name comes from the circuit layout, not the crystal shape.

question: What is the dropout voltage of a linear voltage regulator?
optionA: Minimum input voltage for rated power dissipation
optionB: Maximum output voltage drop when the input voltage is varied over its specified range
optionC: Minimum input-to-output voltage required to maintain regulation
optionD: Maximum that the output voltage may decrease at rated load
explanation: Dropout voltage is the smallest difference between input and output at which a linear regulator can still hold its output steady. If the input falls closer than that, the output drops out of regulation.

question: What occurs when the input signal levels to a mixer are too high?
optionC: Automatic limiting occurs
optionD: Excessive AGC voltage levels are generated
explanation: When a mixer is overdriven, its nonlinear operation creates many unwanted spurious products at combinations of the input frequencies and their harmonics. These show up as spurs and intermodulation in the output.

question: Why is an anti-aliasing filter required in a decimator?
optionA: It removes high-frequency signal components that would otherwise be reproduced as lower frequency components
optionB: It peaks the response of the decimator, improving bandwidth
optionC: It removes low-frequency signal components to eliminate the need for DC restoration
optionD: It notches out the sampling frequency to avoid sampling errors
explanation: After decimation the lower sample rate can only represent lower frequencies. Any components above the new Nyquist limit would fold back as false lower-frequency signals, so a low-pass anti-aliasing filter removes them first.

question: What type of frequency synthesizer circuit uses a phase accumulator, lookup table, digital-to-analog converter, and a low-pass anti-alias filter?
optionC: A phase-locked loop synthesizer
explanation: A direct digital synthesizer uses a phase accumulator stepping through a lookup table of waveform values, a DAC to turn those values into voltage, and a low-pass filter to remove sampling images. A PLL instead uses a VCO and phase detector.

question: What is a truth table?
optionA: A list of inputs and corresponding outputs for an op-amp
optionB: A list of inputs and corresponding outputs for a digital device
optionC: A diagram showing logic states when the digital gate output is true
optionD: A table of logic symbols that indicate the logic states of an op-amp
explanation: A truth table lists every combination of inputs to a digital device and the output each combination produces. It describes logic gates and similar circuits, not op-amps, which are analog.

question: Which of the following filters is used in a 2-meter band repeater duplexer?
optionC: A DSP filter
explanation: A repeater duplexer must notch out the transmitter's powerful signal at the nearby receive frequency, often only 600 kHz away on 2 meters. Resonant cavity filters have the very high Q and power handling that job needs.

question: Which of the following calculates power dissipated by a series linear voltage regulator?
optionA: Input voltage multiplied by input current
optionB: Input voltage divided by output current
optionC: Voltage difference from input to output multiplied by output current
optionD: Output voltage multiplied by output current
explanation: The pass element drops the difference between input and output while carrying the load current, so it dissipates P = (Vin - Vout) x Iout. Example: (15 - 12) x 2 A = 6 W. Vout x Iout is the power delivered to the load.

question: How does a diode envelope detector function?
optionA: By rectification and filtering of RF signals
optionB: By breakdown of the Zener voltage
optionC: By mixing signals with noise in the transition region of the diode
optionD: By sensing the change of reactance in the diode with respect to frequency
explanation: A diode envelope detector rectifies the RF signal and then an RC filter smooths the result, leaving a voltage that follows the amplitude envelope of an AM signal. Zener breakdown plays no part in it.

question: What aspect of receiver analog-to-digital conversion determines the maximum receive bandwidth of a direct-sampling software defined radio (SDR)?
optionC: Integral non-linearity
explanation: A sampler can represent signals up to half its sample rate, so the sample rate sets the widest bandwidth a direct-sampling SDR can receive at once. The number of bits affects dynamic range, not bandwidth.

question: What information is contained in the lookup table of a direct digital synthesizer (DDS)?
optionA: The phase relationship between a reference oscillator and the output waveform
optionB: Amplitude values that represent the desired waveform
optionC: The phase relationship between a voltage-controlled oscillator and the output waveform
optionD: Frequently used receiver and transmitter frequencies
explanation: The DDS lookup table stores amplitude values for points around one cycle of the desired waveform, usually a sine wave. The phase accumulator selects which value to send to the DAC at each clock tick.

question: What does "positive logic" mean in reference to logic devices?
optionA: The logic devices have high noise immunity
optionB: High voltage represents a 1, low voltage a 0
optionC: The logic circuit is in the "true" condition
optionD: 1s and 0s are defined as different positive voltage levels
explanation: Positive logic means the higher voltage level stands for a logic 1 and the lower level for a logic 0. Negative logic reverses that assignment. It has nothing to do with noise immunity.

question: Which of the following measures a filter's ability to reject signals in adjacent channels?
optionC: Shape factor
explanation: Shape factor is the ratio of a filter's bandwidth at a deep attenuation point, such as 60 dB down, to its bandwidth at a shallow point, such as 6 dB down. The closer it is to 1, the better it rejects adjacent channels.

question: What is the purpose of connecting equal-value resistors across power supply filter capacitors connected in series?
optionA: Equalize the voltage across each capacitor
optionB: Discharge the capacitors when voltage is removed
optionC: Provide a minimum load on the supply
explanation: Equal resistors across series filter capacitors do all three jobs: they split the voltage evenly between the capacitors, bleed off their charge after power is removed for safety, and present a small minimum load to the supply.

question: Which type of detector is used for demodulating SSB signals?
optionC: Product detector
explanation: A product detector mixes the SSB signal with a locally generated carrier (BFO) to recover the audio, replacing the carrier removed at the transmitter. A discriminator is used for FM, not SSB.

question: What sets the minimum detectable signal level for a direct-sampling software defined receiver in the absence of atmospheric or thermal noise?
optionB: Reference voltage level and sample width in bits
optionC: Data storage transfer rate
explanation: The smallest voltage step an ADC can resolve equals its reference voltage divided by 2 raised to the number of bits. With no external noise, a signal smaller than one step cannot be detected, so reference level and sample width set the floor.

question: What are the major spectral impurity components of direct digital synthesizers?
optionC: Spurious signals at discrete frequencies
explanation: A DDS's main spectral impurities are discrete spurious signals, caused by phase truncation, DAC quantization and nonlinearity, and clock images. They appear as narrow spurs rather than as broadband noise.

question: What is the purpose of a step-start circuit in a high-voltage power supply?
optionA: To provide a dual-voltage output for reduced power applications
optionB: To compensate for variations of the incoming line voltage
optionC: To prevent arcing across the input power switch or relay contacts
optionD: To allow the filter capacitors to charge gradually
explanation: A step-start circuit applies power through a resistor at first, which limits the inrush current while large filter capacitors charge gradually. The resistor is then shorted out once the capacitors are mostly charged.

question: Which of the following is generally true of Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters?
optionA: FIR filters can delay all frequency components of the signal by the same amount
optionB: FIR filters are easier to implement for a given set of passband rolloff requirements
optionC: FIR filters can respond faster to impulses
explanation: A symmetric FIR filter has linear phase, meaning it delays every frequency component by the same amount and preserves waveform shape. FIR filters usually need more taps than IIR filters for a given rolloff, and they do not respond faster to impulses.

question: Which of the following ensures that a crystal oscillator operates on the frequency specified by the crystal manufacturer?
optionA: Provide the crystal with a specified parallel inductance
optionB: Provide the crystal with a specified parallel capacitance
optionC: Bias the crystal at a specified voltage
optionD: Bias the crystal at a specified current
explanation: A crystal's parallel resonant frequency depends on the capacitance across it, so the maker calibrates it for a specified load capacitance. Supplying that capacitance makes the oscillator run on the marked frequency.

question: What is the function of taps in a digital signal processing filter?
optionA: To reduce excess signal pressure levels
optionC: Select the point at which baseband signals are generated
optionD: Provide incremental signal delays for filter algorithms
explanation: Taps are the points along a DSP filter's delay line, each holding the sample from one sample period earlier. Each delayed sample is multiplied by a coefficient and summed to form the output.

question: Which of the following is a technique for providing highly accurate and stable oscillators needed for microwave transmission and reception?
optionB: Use a rubidium stabilized reference oscillator
optionC: Use a temperature-controlled high Q dielectric resonator
explanation: All three methods are used at microwave frequencies: locking to a GPS-disciplined reference, using a rubidium atomic standard, and using a temperature-controlled high-Q dielectric resonator all give high accuracy and stability.

question: Which of the following would allow a digital signal processing filter to create a sharper filter response?
optionC: Lower Q
explanation: Adding taps lets the filter use more delayed samples and coefficients, which allows steeper skirts and a sharper response at the cost of more computation and delay. Lowering Q would broaden the response instead.

question: What technique shows that a square wave is made up of a sine wave and its odd harmonics?
optionC: Numerical analysis
explanation: Fourier analysis breaks any repeating waveform into a sum of sine waves at the fundamental and its harmonics. Applied to a square wave, it shows a fundamental plus only odd harmonics, each with amplitude falling as 1/n.

question: What is the modulation index of an FM signal?
optionA: The ratio of frequency deviation to modulating signal frequency
optionB: The ratio of modulating signal amplitude to frequency deviation
optionC: The modulating signal frequency divided by the bandwidth of the transmitted signal
optionD: The bandwidth of the transmitted signal divided by the modulating signal frequency
explanation: FM modulation index is the peak frequency deviation divided by the modulating signal frequency. A larger index means more significant sidebands and a wider signal.

question: What is Quadrature Amplitude Modulation or QAM?
optionA: A technique for digital data compression used in digital television which removes redundancy in the data by comparing bit amplitudes
optionB: Transmission of data by modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency but 90 degrees out of phase
optionC: A method of performing single sideband modulation by shifting the phase of the carrier and modulation components of the signal
optionD: A technique for analog modulation of television video signals using phase modulation and compression
explanation: QAM sends data by amplitude modulating two carriers of the same frequency that are 90 degrees apart, called I and Q. Each symbol is a combination of amplitude and phase, which packs several bits per symbol.

question: Why are received spread spectrum signals resistant to interference?
optionA: Signals not using the spread spectrum algorithm are suppressed in the receiver
optionB: The high power used by a spread spectrum transmitter keeps its signal from being easily overpowered
optionC: Built-in error correction codes minimize interference
optionD: If the receiver detects interference, it will signal the transmitter to change frequencies
explanation: A spread spectrum receiver despreads only the signal using the matching code or hop sequence. Any other signal gets spread out by that process and falls to a low level, so interference is suppressed.

question: Which of the following is a type of analog-to-digital conversion?
optionC: Level shifting
explanation: A successive approximation converter compares the input against a DAC output one bit at a time, from the most significant bit down, homing in on the digital value. The other listed terms are not ADC methods.

question: How does the modulation index of a phase-modulated emission vary with RF carrier frequency?
optionA: It increases as the RF carrier frequency increases
optionB: It decreases as the RF carrier frequency increases
optionC: It varies with the square root of the RF carrier frequency
optionD: It does not depend on the RF carrier frequency
explanation: Modulation index depends only on deviation and the modulating frequency. The carrier frequency itself plays no part, so a PM signal has the same index whether it is on 2 meters or 10 meters.

question: What is the definition of symbol rate in a digital transmission?
optionA: The number of control characters in a message packet
optionB: The maximum rate at which the forward error correction code can make corrections
optionC: The rate at which the waveform changes to convey information
optionD: The number of characters carried per second by the station-to-station link
explanation: Symbol rate is how often the transmitted waveform changes state to carry information, measured in symbols or baud per second. It is not a count of characters or control codes.

question: What spread spectrum communications technique uses a high-speed binary bit stream to shift the phase of an RF carrier?
optionC: Binary phase-shift keying
explanation: Direct sequence spread spectrum uses a fast pseudorandom bit stream to shift the carrier's phase, spreading the signal across a wide bandwidth. Frequency hopping instead moves the carrier between channels.

question: Which of the following describes a signal in the time domain?
optionC: Frequency at different times
explanation: A time-domain view, such as an oscilloscope trace, plots signal amplitude against time. A frequency-domain view, like a spectrum analyzer, instead plots amplitude against frequency.

question: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency deviation of 3000 Hz either side of the carrier frequency if the highest modulating frequency is 1000 Hz?
explanation: Modulation index = deviation / modulating frequency = 3000 Hz / 1000 Hz = 3. Dividing the other way gives 0.33, a common mistake.

question: Why should the phase of a PSK signal be changed at the zero crossing of the RF signal?
optionC: To improve carrier suppression
explanation: Shifting a PSK signal's phase when the RF passes through zero avoids a sudden jump in amplitude. Abrupt transitions create wide sidebands, so switching at zero crossings keeps the signal narrow.

question: Which describes spread spectrum frequency hopping?
optionA: If interference is detected by the receiver, it will signal the transmitter to change frequencies
optionB: RF signals are clipped to generate a wide band of harmonics which provides redundancy to correct errors
optionC: A binary bit stream is used to shift the phase of an RF carrier very rapidly in a pseudorandom sequence
optionD: Rapidly varying the frequency of a transmitted signal according to a pseudorandom sequence
explanation: Frequency hopping moves the carrier rapidly among many frequencies in a pseudorandom pattern known to both ends. The receiver follows the same pattern, so a narrow interferer only hits a few hops.

question: What is "dither" with respect to analog-to-digital converters?
optionA: An abnormal condition where the converter cannot settle on a value to represent the signal
optionB: A small amount of noise added to the input signal to reduce quantization noise
optionC: An error caused by irregular quantization step size
optionD: A method of decimation by randomly skipping samples
explanation: Dither is a small amount of random noise added to the ADC input so that low-level signals cross quantization steps randomly. This spreads the quantization error into broadband noise instead of harmonic distortion.

question: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum carrier deviation of plus or minus 6 kHz if the highest modulating frequency  is 2 kHz?
explanation: Modulation index = deviation / modulating frequency = 6 kHz / 2 kHz = 3. Using the total swing of 12 kHz would wrongly give 6.

question: What technique minimizes the bandwidth of a PSK31 signal?
optionC: Use of sinusoidal data pulses
explanation: PSK31 shapes each phase reversal with a smooth sinusoidal amplitude envelope instead of a hard switch. That gentle shaping keeps sidebands tight, giving the mode its roughly 31 Hz bandwidth.

question: What is the primary effect of extremely short rise or fall time on a CW signal?
optionC: The generation of key clicks
explanation: Keying a CW signal on or off too abruptly creates wide sidebands heard as clicks on nearby frequencies. These key clicks are near the operating frequency, not harmonics at multiples of it.

question: What is the benefit of making voltage measurements with a true-RMS calculating meter?
optionA: An inverse Fourier transform can be used
optionB: The signal's RMS noise factor is also calculated
optionC: The calculated RMS value can be converted directly into phasor form
optionD: RMS is measured for both sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal signals
explanation: A true-RMS meter computes the heating value of the waveform directly, so it reads correctly for square waves, pulses and noise as well as sine waves. Average-responding meters are only accurate for pure sine waves.

question: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3 kHz?
explanation: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation / highest modulating frequency = 5 kHz / 3 kHz = 1.67. Inverting the ratio gives 0.6, which is wrong.

question: What is the approximate bandwidth of a 13-WPM International Morse Code transmission?
optionC: 52 Hz
explanation: A common rule estimates CW bandwidth at about 4 times the speed in words per minute: 13 WPM x 4 = 52 Hz. Clean keying with proper rise and fall times keeps the signal near that width.

question: What is the most common method of reducing key clicks?
optionA: Increase keying waveform rise and fall times
optionB: Insert low-pass filters at the transmitter output
optionC: Reduce keying waveform rise and fall times
optionD: Insert high-pass filters at the transmitter output
explanation: Slowing the rise and fall of each keyed element, often with a shaping network, narrows the signal and removes key clicks. Making the edges faster would worsen them, and output filters cannot remove nearby sidebands.

question: What is the approximate ratio of PEP-to-average power in an unprocessed single-sideband phone signal?
optionC: 1 to 1
explanation: Normal speech has brief peaks and long low-level stretches, so the peak envelope power of unprocessed SSB voice runs roughly 2.5 times the average power. Speech processing raises the average and shrinks that ratio.

question: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 7.5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3.5 kHz?
explanation: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation / highest modulating frequency = 7.5 kHz / 3.5 kHz = 2.14. The inverted value, 0.47, is a common error.

question: What is the bandwidth of an FT8 signal?
optionC: 600 Hz
explanation: An FT8 signal uses 8-tone frequency shift keying with tones 6.25 Hz apart, so it occupies about 50 Hz. Many FT8 stations fit side by side within a single 3 kHz audio passband.

question: What is the advantage of including parity bits in ASCII characters?
optionC: A larger character set is available
optionD: Some types of errors can be detected
explanation: A parity bit makes the count of 1 bits in each character even or odd, so the receiver can spot a single flipped bit. It detects some errors but cannot correct them and adds no speed.

question: What determines the PEP-to-average power ratio of an unprocessed single-sideband phone signal?
optionA: The frequency of the modulating signal
optionC: The degree of carrier suppression
explanation: In SSB the RF envelope follows the voice, so the peak-to-average ratio is set by how speech varies in loudness, with peaks, pauses and syllable dynamics. Carrier suppression and amplifier gain do not change that ratio.

question: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is a technique used for which types of amateur communication?
optionC: EME
optionD: OFDM signals are not allowed on amateur bands
explanation: OFDM spreads data across many closely spaced subcarriers and is used by amateur digital modes and high-speed data links. It is a legal and common digital technique on the ham bands.

question: What is the bandwidth of a 4,800-Hz frequency shift, 9,600-baud ASCII FM transmission?
optionC: 4.8 kHz
explanation: FSK bandwidth = (K x shift) + baud rate, with K = 1.2. So BW = (1.2 x 4800) + 9600 = 5760 + 9600 = 15,360 Hz, or 15.36 kHz. Using the shift or baud rate alone understates the width.

question: What is a common cause of overmodulation of AFSK signals?
optionC: Bit errors in the modem
explanation: Driving the transmitter with too much audio pushes the AFSK signal into distortion, producing extra tones and splatter. Keeping audio below the point where ALC acts avoids overmodulation.

question: Why are direct or flash conversion analog-to-digital converters used for a software defined radio?
optionA: Very low power consumption decreases frequency drift
optionB: Immunity to out-of-sequence coding reduces spurious responses
optionC: Very high speed allows digitizing high frequencies
explanation: A direct or flash ADC compares the input against all reference levels at once, so it converts extremely fast. That speed lets an SDR sample RF signals directly. Flash converters actually draw a lot of power, so low power is not their benefit.

question: What describes orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)?
optionA: A frequency modulation technique that uses non-harmonically related frequencies
optionB: A bandwidth compression technique using Fourier transforms
optionC: A digital mode for narrow-band, slow-speed transmissions
optionD: A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference
explanation: OFDM sends data on many subcarriers spaced so each is orthogonal to the others. That spacing lets them overlap without interfering, and slow symbols on each carrier resist intersymbol interference from multipath.

question: How does ARQ accomplish error correction?
optionA: Special binary codes provide automatic correction
optionB: Special polynomial codes provide automatic correction
optionC: If errors are detected, redundant data is substituted
optionD: If errors are detected, a retransmission is requested
explanation: ARQ (automatic repeat request) checks each received block for errors and, if one is found, asks the sender to transmit that block again. Forward error correction, by contrast, fixes errors without a resend.

question: What parameter evaluates distortion of an AFSK signal caused by excessive input audio levels?
optionC: Repeat Request Rate (RRR)
explanation: Intermodulation distortion measures the unwanted products created when the AFSK or PSK tones are overdriven. Excess audio raises IMD, which widens the signal and degrades decoding.

question: How many different input levels can be encoded by an analog-to-digital converter with 8-bit resolution?
optionB: 8 multiplied by the gain of the input amplifier
optionC: 256 divided by the gain of the input amplifier
explanation: An n-bit converter can output 2^n distinct codes. With 8 bits that is 2^8 = 256 levels. Input amplifier gain changes which voltages map to each code, not how many codes exist.

question: What is deviation ratio?
optionA: The ratio of the audio modulating frequency to the center carrier frequency
optionB: The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency
optionC: The ratio of the carrier center frequency to the audio modulating frequency
optionD: The ratio of the highest audio modulating frequency to the average audio modulating frequency
explanation: Deviation ratio is the maximum carrier deviation divided by the highest audio modulating frequency the system allows. It is the worst-case modulation index used to size an FM channel.

question: Which digital code allows only one bit to change between sequential code values?
optionB: Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
optionC: Extended ASCII
explanation: In Gray code, consecutive values differ by only one bit, which avoids large errors when a value is read during a transition, as in shaft encoders. Binary coded decimal and ASCII can change several bits at once.

question: What is considered an acceptable maximum IMD level for an idling PSK signal?
optionC: +15 dB
explanation: An idling PSK31 signal is two tones, and a clean transmitter keeps the third-order IMD products about 30 dB or more below them. Readings like -20 dB show overdriven audio and splatter.

question: What is the purpose of a low-pass filter used at the output of a digital-to-analog converter?
optionA: Lower the input bandwidth to increase the effective resolution
optionB: Improve accuracy by removing out-of-sequence codes from the input
optionC: Remove spurious sampling artifacts from the output signal
explanation: A DAC output is a stepped waveform that carries images and artifacts near multiples of the sample rate. A low-pass reconstruction filter removes those artifacts and leaves a smooth analog signal.

question: What is frequency division multiplexing (FDM)?
optionA: The transmitted signal jumps from band to band at a predetermined rate
optionB: Dividing the transmitted signal into separate frequency bands that each carry a different data stream
optionC: The transmitted signal is divided into packets of information
optionD: Two or more information streams are merged into a digital combiner, which then pulse position modulates the transmitter
explanation: Frequency division multiplexing splits the available bandwidth into separate subbands, each carrying its own data stream at the same time. Jumping between bands would be frequency hopping, not FDM.

question: How can data rate be increased without increasing bandwidth?
optionC: Using a more efficient digital code
explanation: A more efficient code, such as one carrying more bits per symbol or using variable-length characters, moves more data in the same symbol rate and bandwidth. Adding forward error correction uses capacity rather than adding it.

question: What are some of the differences between the Baudot digital code and ASCII?
optionA: Baudot uses 4 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 1 character as a letters/figures shift code, ASCII has no letters/figures code
optionB: Baudot uses 5 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot uses 2 characters as letters/figures shift codes, ASCII has no letters/figures shift code
optionC: Baudot uses 6 data bits per character, ASCII uses 7 or 8; Baudot has no letters/figures shift code, ASCII uses 2 letters/figures shift codes
optionD: Baudot uses 7 data bits per character, ASCII uses 8; Baudot has no letters/figures shift code, ASCII uses 2 letters/figures shift codes
explanation: Baudot uses 5 data bits per character and relies on letters and figures shift codes to double its small character set. ASCII uses 7 or 8 bits, so it has room for every character without shift codes.

question: Which of the following is a measure of the quality of an analog-to-digital converter?
optionC: Reciprocal mixing
explanation: Total harmonic distortion shows how faithfully a converter reproduces a pure tone, so it is a standard measure of ADC quality. Peak envelope power and power factor describe transmitters and loads, not converters.

question: What is digital time division multiplexing?
optionA: Two or more data streams are assigned to discrete sub-carriers on an FM transmitter
optionB: Two or more signals are arranged to share discrete time slots of a data transmission
optionC: Two or more data streams share the same channel by transmitting time of transmission as the sub-carrier
optionD: Two or more signals are quadrature modulated to increase bandwidth efficiency
explanation: Time division multiplexing gives each signal its own repeating time slot in one data stream, so several channels share a link by taking turns. Separate subcarriers would be frequency division instead.

question: What is the relationship between symbol rate and baud?
optionB: Baud is twice the symbol rate
optionC: Baud rate is half the symbol rate
optionD: The relationship depends on the specific code used
explanation: Baud is the unit for symbol rate: one baud equals one symbol per second. The bit rate can differ from the baud rate when each symbol carries several bits, but baud and symbol rate are the same thing.

question: What is one advantage of using ASCII code for data communications?
optionA: It includes built-in error correction features
optionB: It contains fewer information bits per character than any other code
optionC: It is possible to transmit both uppercase and lowercase text
optionD: It uses one character as a shift code to send numeric and special characters
explanation: ASCII has enough code values to carry both uppercase and lowercase letters plus symbols, unlike 5-bit Baudot. It has no built-in error correction, and it needs no shift character.

question: What factors affect the bandwidth of a transmitted CW signal?
optionC: Keying speed and shape factor (rise and fall time)
explanation: CW bandwidth depends on how fast you send and how sharply each element turns on and off. Faster keying and steeper rise and fall times both widen the signal. Receiver IF bandwidth and Q do not affect what is transmitted.

question: What is described by the constellation diagram of a QAM or QPSK signal?
optionA: How many carriers may be present at the same time
optionB: The possible phase and amplitude states for each symbol
optionC: Frequency response of the signal stream
optionD: The number of bits used for error correction in the protocol
explanation: A constellation diagram plots each allowed symbol as a point on the I/Q plane, where distance from center is amplitude and angle is phase. It shows every possible phase and amplitude state of a QAM or QPSK symbol.

question: What type of addresses do nodes have in a mesh network?
optionC: Internet Protocol (IP)
explanation: Amateur mesh networks such as AREDN carry ordinary internet protocol traffic, so each node is identified by an IP address. Talk groups belong to digital voice systems, not mesh data networks.

question: What technique do individual nodes use to form a mesh network?
optionA: Forward error correction and Viterbi codes
optionC: Discovery and link establishment protocols
optionD: Custom code plugs for the local trunking systems
explanation: Mesh nodes find their neighbors with discovery protocols and then set up links and routes automatically, so the network forms and heals itself. Store-and-forward digipeating is a packet radio technique, not mesh formation.

question: What is an isotropic radiator?
optionA: A calibrated, unidirectional antenna used to make precise antenna gain measurements
optionB: An omnidirectional, horizontally polarized, precisely calibrated antenna used to make field measurements of antenna gain
optionC: A hypothetical, lossless antenna having equal radiation intensity in all directions used as a reference for antenna gain
optionD: A spacecraft antenna used to direct signals toward Earth
explanation: An isotropic radiator is an imaginary lossless antenna that radiates equally in every direction. It cannot be built, but it serves as the reference for gain figures quoted in dBi.

question: What is the difference in radiated power between a lossless antenna with gain and an isotropic radiator driven by the same power?
optionA: The power radiated from the directional antenna is increased by the gain of the antenna
optionB: The power radiated from the directional antenna is stronger by its front-to-back ratio
optionC: They are the same
optionD: The power radiated from the isotropic radiator is 2.15 dB greater than that from the directional antenna
explanation: Gain only redirects power; it does not create any. A lossless directional antenna and an isotropic radiator fed the same power radiate the same total power, the directional one simply concentrates it.

question: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2-wavelength apart and fed 180 degrees out of phase?
optionC: A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
optionD: A figure-eight oriented along the axis of the array
explanation: With half-wave spacing and 180-degree phasing, signals cancel broadside and add along the line joining the verticals. The result is a figure-eight pattern pointing along the array axis, called end-fire.

question: How much does the gain of an ideal parabolic reflector antenna increase when the operating frequency is doubled?
optionC: 4 dB
explanation: A dish's gain rises with the square of frequency for a fixed size. Doubling frequency multiplies gain by 4, and 10 x log10(4) = 6.02, about 6 dB.

question: Which matching system for Yagi antennas requires the driven element to be insulated from the boom?
optionC: Shunt-fed
explanation: In a beta or hairpin match, the hairpin is connected across a split driven element, so each half must be insulated from the boom. Gamma and T matches attach to a continuous element that can be grounded to the boom.

question: What is the velocity factor of a transmission line?
optionA: The ratio of its characteristic impedance to its termination impedance
optionB: The ratio of its termination impedance to its characteristic impedance
optionC: The velocity of a wave in the transmission line multiplied by the velocity of light in a vacuum
optionD: The velocity of a wave in the transmission line divided by the velocity of light in a vacuum
explanation: Velocity factor is the speed of a wave in the transmission line divided by the speed of light in a vacuum. Solid polyethylene coax is about 0.66, while open-wire line is close to 1.

question: Which of the following can be calculated using a Smith chart?
optionC: Antenna radiation pattern
explanation: A Smith chart maps impedance and lets you track how it changes moving along a transmission line. It does not handle radiation patterns, radiation resistance or propagation.

question: When constructing a Beverage antenna, which of the following factors should be included in the design to achieve good performance at the desired frequency?
optionA: Its overall length must not exceed 1/4 wavelength
optionB: It must be mounted more than 1 wavelength above ground
optionC: It should be configured as a four-sided loop
optionD: It should be at least one wavelength long
explanation: A Beverage is a long, low wire that works by traveling waves, and it needs to be at least about one wavelength long for useful directivity. Longer Beverages give narrower patterns.

question: What is the effective radiated power (ERP) of a repeater station with 150 watts transmitter power output, 2 dB feed line loss, 2.2 dB duplexer loss, and 7 dBd antenna gain?
optionC: 420 watts
explanation: Add the decibels first: net gain = 7 dBd - 2 dB - 2.2 dB = 2.8 dB. ERP = 150 W x 10^(2.8/10) = 150 x 1.905 = about 286 watts. Forgetting the duplexer loss gives too high a figure.

question: What is the far field of an antenna?
optionA: The region of the ionosphere where radiated power is not refracted
optionB: The region where radiated power dissipates over a specified time period
optionC: The region where radiated field strengths are constant
optionD: The region where the shape of the radiation pattern no longer varies with distance
explanation: The far field begins several wavelengths out, where the pattern shape stays the same as distance grows and field strength simply falls off with distance. Closer in, the reactive near field distorts it.

question: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/4-wavelength apart and fed 90 degrees out of phase?
optionB: A figure-eight end-fire along the axis of the array
optionC: A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
explanation: Quarter-wave spacing with 90-degree phasing makes signals add in one direction along the axis and cancel in the other. The result is a cardioid with a single deep null off the back.

question: How can two linearly polarized Yagi antennas be used to produce circular polarization?
optionA: Stack two Yagis to form an array with the respective elements in parallel planes fed 90 degrees out of phase
optionB: Stack two Yagis to form an array with the respective elements in parallel planes fed in phase
optionC: Arrange two Yagis on the same axis and perpendicular to each other with the driven elements at the same point on the boom and fed 90 degrees out of phase
optionD: Arrange two Yagis collinear to each other with the driven elements fed 180 degrees out of phase
explanation: Two Yagis mounted at right angles on one boom, with driven elements at the same point and fed 90 degrees apart, produce circular polarization. The 90-degree phase shift between perpendicular fields makes the field rotate.

question: What antenna matching system matches coaxial cable to an antenna by connecting the shield to the center of the antenna and the conductor a fraction of a wavelength to one side?
optionC: T-match
explanation: A gamma match ties the coax shield to the element's center and the inner conductor to a rod that taps the element a short distance to one side. A series capacitor then tunes out the rod's inductance.

question: Which of the following has the biggest effect on the velocity factor of a transmission line?
optionC: The insulating dielectric material
explanation: The insulating dielectric slows the wave; velocity factor is about 1 divided by the square root of the dielectric constant. Line length and impedance do not set it.

question: What type of coordinate system is used in a Smith chart?
optionC: Voltage chords and current chords
explanation: A Smith chart uses circles of constant resistance and arcs of constant reactance. Every impedance falls where one resistance circle and one reactance arc cross.

question: Which is generally true for 160- and 80-meter receiving antennas?
optionA: Atmospheric noise is so high that directivity is much more important than losses
optionB: They must be erected at least 1/2 wavelength above the ground to attain good directivity
optionC: Low loss coax transmission line is essential for good performance
explanation: On 160 and 80 meters, atmospheric noise is so strong that a lossy receive antenna still hears well above the receiver's own noise. What matters most is directivity to reject noise from other directions.

question: What term describing total radiated power takes into account all gains and losses?
optionC: Effective radiated power
explanation: Effective radiated power combines transmitter output with all feed line and component losses and the antenna gain to give the power effectively sent in the favored direction.

question: What type of analysis is commonly used for modeling antennas?
optionC: Mutual impedance analysis
optionD: Calculus differentiation with respect to physical properties
explanation: Antenna modeling programs such as NEC and MININEC use the Method of Moments, which solves for current along the antenna wires. From those currents they compute patterns, gain and impedance.

question: What type of radiation pattern is created by two 1/4-wavelength vertical antennas spaced 1/2-wavelength apart and fed in phase?
optionC: A figure-eight broadside to the axis of the array
optionD: A figure-eight end-fire along the axis of the array
explanation: Fed in phase and spaced a half wavelength, the two verticals add broadside and cancel along the line joining them. That gives a figure-eight pattern broadside to the array axis.

question: What is the most efficient location for a loading coil on an electrically short whip?
optionA: Near the center of the vertical radiator
optionB: As low as possible on the vertical radiator
optionC: At a voltage maximum
explanation: Placing the loading coil near the middle of a short whip lets more current flow in the lower radiating section than a base coil allows. That raises radiation resistance and efficiency.

question: What matching system uses a short length of transmission line connected in parallel with the feed line at or near the feed point?
optionC: T-match
explanation: A stub match uses a short section of transmission line, open or shorted, connected in parallel with the feed line near the load. Its reactance cancels the load reactance to give a match.

question: Why is the electrical length of a coaxial cable longer than its physical length?
optionA: Skin effect is less pronounced in the coaxial cable
optionB: Skin effect is more pronounced in the coaxial cable
optionC: Electromagnetic waves move faster in coaxial cable than in air
optionD: Electromagnetic waves move more slowly in a coaxial cable than in air
